sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not touch on an IA or Extended Essay
paragraphs: This is the line that separates legitimate tutoring from a service that can get a student's diploma withheld. Under IB academic-honesty rules the Internal Assessment, Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge essay must be the student's own work, authenticated by the supervising teacher. A tutor may teach the criteria, question the method, challenge the reasoning and give feedback on a draft the student has written. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite paragraphs to completion, or hand over a worked investigation for the student to submit.

The distinction is easy to apply in practice once it is stated. Teaching what Criterion C rewards in a Mathematics exploration is instruction. Explaining why a chosen research question cannot be answered with the data available is instruction. Pointing out that a paragraph asserts a conclusion the evidence does not support is feedback. Producing the corrected paragraph is not feedback, and no amount of framing makes it so. One site in this market openly sells completed Internal Assessments; a family who buys one is buying an academic-misconduct finding with a document attached.

Criteria knowledge is where honest support pays off most, because the marks are published and specific. A Mathematics exploration is assessed across five criteria covering presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics, with different mark allocations and a combined total of twenty, and the component contributes a fifth of the subject grade. The Extended Essay is marked across criteria covering focus and method, knowledge and understanding, critical thinking, presentation and engagement. Students routinely lose marks on the criteria that reward process, because nobody has shown them that reflection is assessed.

Our position is published because it is a differentiator in this market rather than a disclaimer. IB Gram's tutors do not write any part of assessed coursework, do not supply model answers to be submitted, and do not distribute board syllabus documents, past papers or mark schemes as downloads; those are the boards' copyright and should be read from the boards' own sites. If a provider offers more than that, the thing being sold is risk.

sections.heading: ADEK, inspection ratings, and reading a school report honestly
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi private schools are regulated by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. This is worth knowing for two reasons: it is the authority whose published ratings tell you something checkable about a school, and it is the body whose professional-conduct rules bear on who may tutor your child. ADEK is named by none of the competing tutoring pages in the research set, which is a strange gap on pages written for Abu Dhabi parents.

Across the UAE the regulator map is worth having straight. Dubai's private schools answer to the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Sharjah's are regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and Ras Al Khaimah's by its Department of Knowledge; both of those authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the ministry's general regulations.

On who may tutor, the relevant facts are federal. Private tuition in the UAE is regulated through a MoHRE work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no figure should be quoted to you.

There is an Abu Dhabi-specific point parents ask about often. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with teachers tutoring outside school hours required to hold the MoHRE private tuition permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. Treat that as press-reported rather than quoted policy, and verify it against ADEK's current published document before acting on it. The practical reading is simple: your child's own classroom teacher is not the right person to hire privately.

process.title: Tell us the specification, not just the subject
process.description: Send the syllabus code from the statement of entry or the school's subject guide, the tier or level, and the next assessment date. A request that says Cambridge Chemistry 0620 Extended, mock in six weeks is actionable immediately. A request that says help with science takes two more emails to become useful.

process.title: Free trial lesson and a written diagnostic
process.description: The first session is a free trial run on real questions from the student's own specification. It ends with a written note of the two or three things costing the most marks and what the first month would target. The trial is free with no card required; if the match is wrong, say so and nothing follows.

process.title: A plan counted back from the exam date
process.description: Sessions are sequenced from the assessment date backwards, not from the start of the textbook forwards. That means the entry deadline, the mock window and the school's internal coursework deadlines are in the plan from the first week, and the final weeks are reserved for timed papers rather than new content.

process.title: Weekly teaching with marked work in between
process.description: A fixed slot each week on Gulf Standard Time, with work set and marked between sessions. The tutor keeps an error log so a repeated misconception is visible rather than remembered, and a short written note after each session tells you what was covered and what was set.

process.title: Review every half term, change if it is not working
process.description: At each half term the tutor, the student and you look at marked evidence: paper scores, error-log patterns and the gap to the target grade. If the evidence does not show movement, the sensible response is a different tutor or a different plan, and we will say so rather than sell another block.

whyPoints.title: Syllabus-level teaching, not subject-level
whyPoints.description: A tutor is matched to the specification the student is entered for, including the board and the tier. That sounds administrative until you see the difference between 0580 and 4MA1 revision: one needs non-calculator drilling the other does not. Working from the wrong board's papers is the most common invisible waste in private tuition.

whyPoints.title: A tutor pool that is not limited by a driving radius
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means the Higher Level Chemistry specialist or the Pearson Further Pure Maths teacher can take a session with an Abu Dhabi student regardless of where either of them is. Families in Yas Island and Mohammed Bin Zayed City get the same subject choice as families two streets from a school.

whyPoints.title: Coursework support that stays inside the rules
whyPoints.description: Internal Assessment, Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge work is taught by criterion, questioned and given feedback on. No text is supplied for submission, and no board material is redistributed. That boundary is published here because it is the thing most worth checking before paying anybody in this market.

whyPoints.title: Evidence a parent can inspect
whyPoints.description: Marked papers with the mark scheme applied, an error log carried across sessions, and a short written note after each lesson. Progress claims on this page are deliberately absent; what we offer instead is the marked work, so you can form your own view rather than take ours.

whyPoints.title: Figures with their sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every date and requirement on this page names the board or authority it came from, and anything unverified is marked as such rather than smoothed over. That includes the inconvenient cases: IB examination dates are not published here because they could not be confirmed from the IB itself.

whyPoints.title: A clear answer about delivery
whyPoints.description: Tuition for Abu Dhabi families is online, one to one, over live video with a shared screen. IB Gram does not operate a centre in the UAE and does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi. Saying that plainly saves everybody a phone call, and the comparison tables on this site make the case on merit.

faqs.question: What does an IB and IGCSE tutor in Abu Dhabi actually do in the first session?
faqs.answer: The first session is a diagnostic rather than a lesson. The tutor works through real questions from the student's own specification, at the tier or level the student is entered for, and watches where the answer breaks down: content gaps, command-term mismatch, method marks lost to disordered working, or arithmetic under time pressure. It ends with a written note naming the two or three issues costing the most marks and what the first month of sessions would target. That note is yours whether or not you continue. The trial session is free and no card is required to book it.

faqs.question: Is Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 graded 9 to 1 or A* to G?
faqs.answer: Both scales are in use across Cambridge IGCSE syllabuses, which is why parents get conflicting answers. Some syllabuses report on the 9 to 1 numeric scale and others on A* to G, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE reports on 9 to 1. The only reliable source is the statement of entry or the current syllabus document for the exact code the student is sitting. For planning purposes the useful anchors are that grade 7 is broadly the old A, grade 4 to 5 covers the old C, and grade 3 maps to E, which is the grade the UAE Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency rule names as the minimum for each counted subject.

faqs.question: Should my child sit the Core or the Extended tier in IGCSE science?
faqs.answer: Decide it against the destination, not against last term's confidence. Core tier caps the grade available, so if the next step is a Higher Level Diploma subject or an A-Level in the same science, a capped grade can close that route even when it clears the UAE equivalency floor comfortably. The practical test is how much Extended-only content is genuinely out of reach and how many teaching weeks remain before the final entry deadline. A diagnostic on exactly those topics gives you evidence to take to the head of department. The decision locks at entry, months before the exam.

faqs.question: How much is the alternative-to-practical paper worth in Cambridge IGCSE Physics?
faqs.answer: In the Cambridge IGCSE sciences the practical component, whether sat as a practical test or as the alternative-to-practical written paper, carries roughly a fifth of the total mark, and most international centres use the written route. Check the exact weighting in the current 0625 syllabus document on cambridgeinternational.org, because weightings are revised between syllabus versions. It is the most teachable component on the specification: describing a method reproducibly, identifying variables, spotting anomalous results, reading scales and drawing a line of best fit are all format skills rather than content, and eight to ten marked past-paper questions move the mark noticeably.

faqs.question: My child moves from MYP 5 into DP1 next year. What should we fix first?
faqs.answer: Three things, in this order. Mathematical manipulation speed, because both Diploma mathematics routes and all the sciences assume fluency the Middle Years Programme never tested under time pressure. The specific content gap between what the student's MYP subject covered and what the Diploma subject guide prescribes, which differs by school. And extended-writing stamina for Paper 2 style responses, which are longer than most MYP tasks. A short block of sessions in the months before DP1 starts is worth more than twice as many in November, when the first Internal Assessment deadlines are already moving.

faqs.question: Does the Cambridge entry deadline really fall three months before the exam?
faqs.answer: In the UAE it usually falls further out than that. Your child sits either the June series or the November series, and entries for the June papers close in the spring, roughly four months ahead of the first script rather than three. Read backwards, that means any tier change or subject addition has to be settled before the spring entry closes; after that the only route to a different tier is the November series. The comparable Pearson figure is public and shows the same shape: the International GCSE November 2026 timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, with entries long closed and results reaching students the following January. Deadlines differ by series and by centre, so confirm your child's dates with the examinations officer and work from the official timetable for the centre's administrative zone.

faqs.question: Can a tutor look at my child's Mathematics exploration before it is submitted?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach the assessment criteria, question whether the research question is answerable with the data available, and give feedback on a draft the student has written. A tutor cannot write, rewrite or complete any part of it, and cannot supply text for submission. That boundary comes from IB academic-honesty rules, and the supervising teacher authenticates the work. The useful work is usually criterion knowledge: the exploration is marked across five criteria covering presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics, and students lose marks most often on the ones that assess process.

faqs.question: What does an ADEK inspection rating tell me about my child's IGCSE teaching?
faqs.answer: ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi and publishes inspection outcomes, so a rating is a checkable judgement about the school as a whole. It is not a statement about one department in one year. A school with a strong overall rating can still have a science department that has lost two teachers mid-year, and that is the situation most tutoring requests come from. Read the published report for the subject-level commentary rather than the headline band, and compare it against your child's own marked work.

faqs.question: How many weekly hours does a Year 11 IGCSE student in Abu Dhabi usually need?
faqs.answer: Most families start with one hour a week per subject and add a second hour in the eight to ten weeks before mocks or finals. Beyond two hours a week in a single subject, the limiting factor is usually independent practice rather than teaching time: a student who is not completing marked work between sessions will not convert a third hour into marks. Two subjects at one hour each is a common and workable commitment through an IGCSE year. The realistic planning question is how many weeks remain before the entry deadline and the examination window, not how many hours sound reassuring.

faqs.question: Are Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades treated the same way?
faqs.answer: For the UAE Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency rule, what matters is that the subjects are accredited and meet the stated minimum grade, with five counted subjects required at no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that five. Universities set their own view and may state subject prerequisites rather than board preferences. Where the two boards genuinely differ is in structure: tiering, calculator policy in mathematics and practical assessment are not the same, so revision has to follow the board the student is actually entered for.

faqs.question: My child takes nine IGCSE subjects. How many should we tutor at once?
faqs.answer: Two, in most cases, and rarely more than three. Tutoring four subjects at once produces a timetable with no space for the independent practice that converts teaching into marks, and it is also where family budgets break mid-year, which usually ends the whole arrangement. Choose by consequence rather than by lowest grade: the subject that gates the next step matters more than the subject with the weakest mock. The remaining subjects can be supported with a marked-paper block closer to the examination window rather than a weekly slot all year.

faqs.question: What if nobody covers Pearson Further Pure Mathematics 4PM1 at the level we need?
faqs.answer: We tell you, rather than matching you with somebody adjacent to the subject. Niche requests are where this matters: Pearson Further Pure Mathematics 4PM1, Higher Level Theatre, Arabic as a first language at Diploma level, and Computer Science at Higher Level all have thin specialist supply. In those cases you will be told the realistic wait, offered a specialist who teaches online from outside the UAE, or told plainly that we cannot cover it. Being matched with a tutor who is learning the specification alongside the student is the worst outcome of the three.

faqs.question: How does a tutor mark a past paper if the lessons are online?
faqs.answer: The student photographs or scans their written work and sends it before the session. The tutor marks it against the published mark scheme, then shares the annotated script on screen during the lesson and talks through where each mark was awarded or lost. The marked file stays with the family. In practice this is more useful than marking across a kitchen table, because the annotated script is permanent, searchable and available to the student during revision rather than existing only in that session's memory.

faqs.question: Do we have to commit to a term of IGCSE tutoring in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. Sessions are booked as you go, and most families start with a free trial followed by a four to six week block aimed at one specific thing: a mock, a tier decision, or a paper skill. Longer plans make sense when the target is a grade shift across a full year, because that needs work set and marked between sessions over months. What we would not recommend is paying for a large package before a trial, which is a pattern worth questioning in any provider's pricing, not only ours.

faqs.question: What is the minimum IGCSE grade the UAE counts towards equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track, as reported in July 2026, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must also show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. Equivalency is a Ministry of Education process that no tutoring provider performs or influences, so verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae or with the school's university counsellor before relying on it.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the specification and the next date in the diary
abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB IGCSE tutor in Abu Dhabi, the fastest route to a useful answer is to send three things: the syllabus code and tier or level, the next assessment date, and a photograph of a recent piece of marked work. That is enough for a specialist to say what the real problem is and whether an hour a week will move it. The first session is a free trial and ends with a written diagnostic you keep either way. Lessons run online, one to one, on Gulf Standard Time, and if the subject is one we cannot cover properly we will say so rather than match you with somebody close enough.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-abu-dhabi-i.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE across mathematics, the sciences and the essay subjects, one-to-one over live video into Gulf Standard Time. Sessions are planned against the series your child is actually entered for rather than against a generic revision year.

intro.heading: The year, read backwards from the paper
paragraphs: Almost every mistake families make about IGCSE revision is a calendar mistake. Money gets spent in the wrong month, decisions get raised after the deadline that could have acted on them, and content teaching gets bought at the point in the year when only practice still works. None of that is about effort. It is about a timetable nobody sets out, and which several tutoring pages get wrong for UAE families specifically.

The first thing to get right is which series your child sits. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered to India only. A UAE family planning around a February window is planning for a different country, and that error has appeared on pages aimed at exactly this audience. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November.

The second is the zone. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. That is the board's own language and it is unusually blunt. Your child's school knows which zone it sits in; the right action is to ask rather than to download a timetable and assume.

The third is lead time. Entry deadlines sit months before the paper, and results arrive months after it. For a sense of the distances involved, the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, and June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which is why the live official timetable is always the document to work from rather than any date restated on a tutoring page, including this one.

IB dates are a separate matter and this page does not publish any. The International Baccalaureate's own site returns an error to automated checking, so no IB session or results date in this project has been confirmed from the IB itself. Write to your child's IB coordinator or check ibo.org directly before acting on any IB date you read anywhere, including dates that look authoritative because they appear on several sites at once. Tuition for Abu Dhabi families is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and home visits are a service offered only in India.

programmes.description: Terminal examination in a named series, with entries made by the centre months in advance and tiering decided at the point of entry in the Cambridge routes. Nothing can be banked ahead except coursework where a specification uses it, so the whole plan points at one window.

programmes.description: A mix of internal deadlines set by the school and external deadlines set by the IB, with internal assessment components generating dates from the first term. abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-abu-dhabi-i.subjectsIntro: Each subject below is listed with the calendar fact that matters most for it, because the planning differs. A coursework-bearing subject and a wholly examined one need different Septembers.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge IGCSE 0580)
subjects.description: Wholly examined, no coursework, so everything points at the series. Tier is decided at entry, which makes the autumn of Year 11 the last useful window for a tier conversation backed by a timed script.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: Available in May/June and November. A single-subject November retake is a contained plan for mathematics specifically, because the content is already covered and the remaining work is technique under timing.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge IGCSE 0625)
subjects.description: Theory papers plus a practical or alternative-to-practical component, all sat within the series. The practical component is examined rather than coursework-assessed, so it can be prepared for right up to study leave.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge IGCSE 0620)
subjects.description: Same component structure. The calendar consequence is that a mole gap found in the autumn of Year 10 can be taught properly, and the same gap found in March can only be revised around.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge IGCSE 0610)
subjects.description: The most content-heavy of the three sciences and the most amenable to late revision, because terminology precision moves quickly. A useful subject to leave later in a crowded revision plan.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500 and 0990)
subjects.description: Where a coursework route is used, the deadlines are internal and sit much earlier than the series. Those are the dates to ask about in September, because a missed internal deadline cannot be revised away.

subjects.name: Literature in English (Cambridge 0475 and 0992)
subjects.description: Set texts have to be read on the school's schedule, not a revision schedule. Learning a new set text in the final eight weeks is the least reliable plan available, which is a calendar fact rather than a judgement.

subjects.name: History (Cambridge IGCSE 0470)
subjects.description: Case-study and source work. Source technique is trainable late and case-study knowledge is not, so the two halves of this subject belong in different parts of the revision calendar.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge IGCSE 0478)
subjects.description: Algorithm tracing and pseudocode conventions are technique rather than content, which makes them unusually responsive to work in the final quarter. Worth knowing when triaging a crowded plan.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first or additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory provision alongside any international curriculum under the federal baseline for UAE private schools. Where an IGCSE entry exists, it sits in the same series as everything else and competes for the same revision weeks.

sections.heading: Which series your child actually sits
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests offered in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered to India only. That single sentence resolves most of the confusion on this subject, and it is worth repeating because pages aimed at UAE parents have published the February window and its associated deadlines as though they applied here.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE is available in May/June and November each year. Where a school uses both boards across different subjects, which is common in the UAE, a pupil can have papers governed by two sets of arrangements in the same year. That is manageable and it does mean the question 'when are the exams' has two answers and needs asking twice, once per board.

The practical consequence for an Abu Dhabi family is that the main window is the early summer and the second window is the late autumn. A Year 11 cohort sits June. A pupil who needs one subject again sits November, with results in the following January. There is no mid-year window available to a UAE candidate, which matters because it removes an option families sometimes believe they have when a June result disappoints.

The instruction that follows from all of this is narrow and worth doing in writing. Ask your child's examinations officer which board and specification code each subject is entered for, and which series. Then download the live official timetable from the board's own site. Do not plan from a date restated anywhere else, including here, because Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and both boards revise them.

sections.heading: The six administrative zones, and the board's own warning
paragraphs: This is the part of the calendar most families have never heard of and it carries the sharpest consequence. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones. Timetables are published per zone, because examinations are sat at different local times across the world to protect the integrity of the papers. The board states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone.

It then says something unusually direct for a public examination body: that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. That is not boilerplate. It is the board declining to remedy a specific, foreseeable, entirely avoidable error, and the error is downloading a timetable from a search result rather than asking which zone applies.

A family can eliminate the risk in one email. Ask the examinations officer which administrative zone the centre sits in, and then use the timetable for that zone for every date. Pin it somewhere. If a pupil is working from a printed timetable at home, check that it carries the right zone label. If a tutor has supplied dates, check where they came from. This takes ten minutes once and removes a category of catastrophe.

The same discipline applies to provisional timetables. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which means a date read in one month may be revised by the next. Working from the live official document rather than a copy is therefore a standing rule rather than a one-off check, and it is the reason this page tells you where the documents live instead of listing dates you might rely on.

sections.heading: The June series, counted backwards
paragraphs: Read forwards, a school year looks like a long runway with an examination at the end. Read backwards from the paper, it becomes a sequence of gates, each of which closes something. That is the more useful reading, because it shows which decisions have already been taken by the time most families start worrying and which are still open.

The last gate to close is the entry itself, made by the centre months before the paper. Before that sits the tier decision in the Cambridge routes, which is effectively the grade ceiling. Before that sit the school's mocks, which are the cheapest diagnostic available because somebody else has already administered a timed paper under proper conditions. And before that sits the autumn, which is the only period in which a substantial content gap can be taught rather than revised.

After the entry closes, the remaining levers are technique and practice. That is not a small thing - the eight to twelve weeks before the paper is genuinely productive for timed practice with immediate correction - but it is a different lever from teaching. A family that discovers a content gap in March has discovered it after the window in which it could have been fixed, and the honest plan is to protect the subjects that can still move.

The spending implication is the shape most families get backwards. Money is cheapest and most effective in August and the autumn, least useful in the quiet middle terms, and expensive but necessary in the final quarter when specialist availability tightens from January. Buying evenly across the year pays the same amount for months of very different value.

sections.heading: The November series as a resit route
paragraphs: The November series is a normal plan rather than a failure plan, and treating it as a contingency from the outset changes how a family handles a disappointing June. Cambridge runs IGCSE in June and November; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. A single-subject retake in November is contained: the content is covered, the diagnosis already exists from the June script, and the remaining work is technique under timing.

The timings involved are worth knowing in general shape. The Pearson Edexcel International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For the main summer window, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Those are past dates, cited so the gap between paper and result is visible, and the live official timetable is still the document to plan from.

Read together, those dates define a short and specific decision window. Summer results arrive in August. A November entry has to be made in the weeks after that, through the centre. Which means a family that wants the November option available has roughly a few weeks between receiving a result and committing to a retake, in a period when schools are reopening and everyone is busy. Knowing this in advance is the difference between a decision and a scramble.

One practical caution. Entries go through a centre, and whether a school will enter a pupil for a November retake, and on what terms, is a school matter rather than a board one. Ask the examinations officer in advance - ideally in the spring, not in August - what the school's position is. Where a school will not enter a pupil, a private candidate route through an approved centre may exist, and that has its own costs and deadlines.

sections.heading: Private candidates and entries outside your own school
paragraphs: Most pupils are entered by their own school and never think about the mechanics. A minority need another route: a pupil whose school does not offer a subject, a pupil wanting a November retake their school will not enter, a home-educated candidate, or a pupil who has moved mid-year. In each case the entry has to go through an approved examination centre, and that is a different process with its own deadlines and costs.

Three things change for a private candidate. Fees are charged by the centre rather than absorbed in school fees, so a cost appears in a specific month that no tutoring quote includes. Deadlines are the centre's and are often earlier than a school's internal ones. And components that require supervised practical or coursework arrangements may not be available at every centre, which can restrict which specifications are realistically open.

The practical sequence is to ask early and in writing. Ask your own school first whether it will enter the pupil, because that is simplest if the answer is yes. If it will not, identify approved centres in the emirate and ask each what it enters, by what deadline, at what fee, and whether the components your child's specification requires are available. Then work backwards from the earliest of those deadlines rather than from the examination date.

This also affects what tutoring is useful. A private candidate has no school scheme of work to peg sessions to, which removes the usual anchor and makes the specification itself the only guide. That is a slightly different job from supporting a school-entered pupil, and it is worth saying so when arranging support rather than discovering it in the third session.

sections.heading: After results: enquiries, remarks and what they can do
paragraphs: Results arrive and a small number of them look wrong. Boards operate post-results services through the centre, and the important thing for a family to understand is that these are processes with short deadlines, administered by the school rather than by the candidate, and with outcomes that can move a grade in either direction in some services. Nothing about this is automatic and nothing about it is quick to arrange in late August.

The useful preparation is to know in advance who to ask and how fast. The examinations officer is the route, the deadline is set by the board and is typically weeks rather than months after results, and the first step is usually obtaining the script or a review of marking rather than disputing a grade directly. A family that has already asked, in the spring, how the school handles post-results requests will move considerably faster in August than one working it out from scratch.

It is worth being realistic about what a review achieves. Most marks are correct. Where a grade sits one or two marks below a boundary, a review is a rational thing to request. Where it sits fifteen marks below, a review will almost certainly confirm the mark and the better use of the same weeks is a November entry. Reading the script tells you which situation you are in, which is why asking for the script matters more than any opinion about the grade.

None of this is something a tutoring provider performs or guarantees. The process belongs to the board and the centre. What outside support can do is help read a returned script and decide whether a November entry is worth making, and that is a useful and bounded job. Anyone offering to handle a results enquiry on a family's behalf is offering something they are not party to.

sections.heading: Revision planned against the calendar, not against anxiety
paragraphs: Anxiety produces a predictable and inefficient revision plan: everything, in order, starting with chapter one, intensifying in April. The calendar produces a different one. Different interventions work at different distances from the paper, and matching the two is worth more than any amount of additional hours bought at the wrong moment.

At a year out, content teaching works and nothing else is urgent. At two terms out, content repair still works and mock evidence becomes available. At one term out, technique installation works - the analysis sentence, written method, the units check - because the pupil is changing how they answer rather than learning new facts. At eight weeks, timed practice with immediate correction works. At two weeks, only practice and sleep work, and new content actively harms by displacing consolidation.

Two Abu Dhabi factors shape this. Specialist availability tightens from January as the June series approaches, so the same teaching is harder to book and firmer in price in February than in September. And in some years the heaviest revision quarter overlaps Ramadan, when school days shorten and evenings restructure around Iftar. Moving sessions to a post-Iftar slot keeps the quarter intact; pausing for six weeks removes the most valuable period in the two-year course.

The triage principle for a crowded plan follows from all of this. Leave the subjects where late work is effective until late - biology terminology, Computer Science pseudocode conventions, History source technique, English analysis. Deal early with the subjects where content must be taught - chemistry moles, physics algebra, literature set texts. That ordering is counter-intuitive because it defers the subjects that feel most alarming, and it is what the calendar supports.

sections.heading: What a tutor may not do, and what cannot be promised
paragraphs: Calendar work does not change the rules. A tutor teaches, questions, models on a different example and marks the pupil's own work. A tutor does not write, co-write or edit any submitted piece, including coursework where a specification uses it. One page ranking in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price, which is a malpractice trigger whose exposure falls on the candidate whose certificate is at stake.

Nor should board material be handed over as files. Cambridge, Pearson and the IB own their timetables, syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables. Linking the official page is both the lawful behaviour and the practically better one, because a family that knows where the live timetable lives can check a date themselves rather than relying on a copy that may already be superseded.

Nothing about a calendar can be promised either. No tutor can promise a grade, a score or an improvement, and no provider influences an entry deadline, a zone allocation, a results date or a post-results outcome. Those belong to the boards and the centre. A page implying otherwise has overstated its position, and a provider offering to handle an entry or an enquiry on a family's behalf is offering something it is not party to.

On credentials: IB Gram holds no ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership and makes no such claim. It has no office or centre in Abu Dhabi. Parents may check the one credential that exists - the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with MoHRE's service page listing no fee and a two-working-day completion time.

sections.heading: Coverage, scheduling and the first session
paragraphs: Mathematics, the sciences and the essay subjects at both Cambridge and Pearson tiers are well covered in this set, and a match is usually quick. Thinner briefs exist: Computer Science 0478 with pseudocode conventions, Additional Mathematics 0606, Arabic as a first language, and support for a private candidate working without a school scheme of work. In a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free.

Three outcomes are possible and a family should be told which applies. The brief is covered and a trial lesson is scheduled within days. The brief is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which is disclosed rather than concealed behind a local-looking telephone number. Or the brief is not currently covered, in which case it is named. Rates do not change because a tutor is based outside the UAE.

Scheduling in Abu Dhabi has its own constraint and it bites hardest in the final quarter. Pupils from Khalifa City, Al Raha and the mainland corridors are home late, which makes weekday timed papers unreliable and pushes full sittings to weekends. In the eight to twelve weeks before the series, when a family may want three sessions a week, that distinction determines what is actually achievable rather than what sounds achievable in January.

The first session is free, is one session, and requires no card details. The useful things to bring are the board and specification code for each subject from the examinations officer, the centre's administrative zone, and your child's last marked script. With those three, the remaining weeks can be planned against what actually works at that distance from the paper rather than against the order of the textbook.

process.title: Get the board, the code and the series in writing
process.description: Ask the examinations officer which board and specification code each subject is entered for, at which tier, and in which series. A school using both Cambridge and Pearson across subjects means the question has two answers. A prospectus naming only subjects has not told you what your child is sitting.

process.title: Ask which administrative zone the centre sits in
process.description: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones and publishes timetables per zone, stating that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. One email removes that risk permanently. Check any printed timetable at home carries the right zone label.

process.title: Work from the live official timetable only
process.description: Download it from cambridgeinternational.org or qualifications.pearson.com rather than relying on a restated date. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so dates can be revised, and no IB date should be used at all without confirming it with your child's IB coordinator or on ibo.org.

process.title: Match the intervention to the distance
process.description: Content teaching at a year or two terms out. Technique installation at one term. Timed practice with immediate correction at eight weeks. Practice and sleep at two. Buying content teaching in April is the single most common calendar error, and it is sold readily because it is what an anxious family asks for.

process.title: Ask about November before results, not after
process.description: Find out in the spring whether your school will enter a pupil for a November retake and on what terms, because the decision window after August results is only a few weeks long. Where a school will not, identify approved centres and their deadlines, fees and available components in advance.

whyPoints.title: The right series named for a UAE candidate
whyPoints.description: Cambridge runs June and November here; the February/March series is offered in India only, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Pages aimed at UAE parents have published the February window and its deadlines, and a date a parent acts on is worse than a thin page.

whyPoints.title: The zone rule stated with the board's own warning
whyPoints.description: Cambridge allocates centres to six administrative zones and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. That is the board's language, it is unusually blunt, and it is removed by a single email to the examinations officer.

whyPoints.title: Official documents linked, not restated
whyPoints.description: Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so any date can be revised. The live board document is the only safe source, and a page that lists dates for you to rely on has created a liability rather than a service.

whyPoints.title: No IB date published at all
whyPoints.description: The IB's own site could not be checked by automated means, so no IB session or results date appears here. Confirm every IB date with your child's coordinator or on ibo.org, and treat any IB date on any tutoring page as unverified until you have.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and coverage stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are an India-only service. Where a brief such as private-candidate support has no specialist free, it is named rather than filled with a generalist.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what nobody controls
whyPoints.description: No provider influences an entry deadline, a zone allocation, a results date or a post-results outcome, and none performs or guarantees an entry or an enquiry. Those belong to the boards and the centre, and anyone offering to handle them is offering something they are not party to.

faqs.question: Which exam series does an Abu Dhabi International School pupil actually sit?
faqs.answer: Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, and the February/March series is offered to India only. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE is available in May/June and November. Where a school uses both boards across different subjects, which is common in the UAE, the question has two answers and needs asking twice. Ask the examinations officer for the board, specification code and series for each subject in writing, then work from the board's own live timetable.

faqs.question: Is there any mid-year exam window available to a UAE candidate?
faqs.answer: No. The February/March Cambridge series is offered in India only, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. So a UAE pupil has the early-summer window and the late-autumn one, and nothing between them. That matters because families sometimes believe a mid-year option exists when a June result disappoints, and planning on it wastes the weeks that could have gone into a November entry instead. Pages aimed at UAE parents have published the February window, which is simply the wrong country's calendar.

faqs.question: What are Cambridge's administrative zones and why do they matter?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes timetables per zone, because examinations are sat at different local times around the world. The board states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and adds that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. That is unusually blunt language from an examination body, and the risk is removed by one email asking the examinations officer which zone the centre sits in.

faqs.question: How far ahead of the paper does the entry deadline sit?
faqs.answer: Months, and it is made by the centre rather than by the candidate. The practical consequence is that the tier decision in the Cambridge routes, which sets the grade ceiling, is effectively taken before the entry closes, so evidence intended to influence it has to exist by then. For a sense of overall lead times, the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026 with results reaching students in January. Always use the live official timetable rather than a restated date.

faqs.question: When do IGCSE results reach students in the UAE?
faqs.answer: For the summer window, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. For the autumn window, November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, and the November 2026 series had results reaching students in January. Those are past dates cited so the gap between paper and result is visible. Check the live board timetable for the current series, because Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each one and dates can be revised.

faqs.question: Is a November retake a reasonable plan or a last resort?
faqs.answer: A normal plan, and treating it as a contingency from the start changes how a disappointing August feels. A single-subject retake is contained: the content is already covered, the diagnosis exists in the June script, and the remaining work is technique under timing. The constraint is the decision window, which is only a few weeks between results arriving and an entry being made, in a period when schools are reopening. Ask the examinations officer in the spring what the school's November policy is, not in August.

faqs.question: What if our school will not enter our child for a November paper?
faqs.answer: Then a private candidate route through an approved examination centre may exist, and it works differently. Fees are charged by the centre rather than absorbed in school fees, so a cost lands in a specific month that no tutoring quote includes. Centre deadlines are often earlier than a school's internal ones. And not every centre offers every component, particularly where supervised practical or coursework arrangements are required, so a specification may not be realistically open. Ask each centre what it enters, by when, at what fee, and with which components.

faqs.question: Can anything be done if a grade looks wrong?
faqs.answer: Boards operate post-results services through the centre, with deadlines typically measured in weeks after results rather than months. The route is the examinations officer, and the sensible first step is obtaining the script or a review of marking rather than disputing a grade directly. Be realistic: where a grade sits one or two marks below a boundary a review is rational, and where it sits fifteen marks below the same weeks are better spent on a November entry. Reading the script tells you which case you are in.

faqs.question: Why is buying content teaching in April a mistake?
faqs.answer: Because different interventions work at different distances from the paper, and teaching is not one of the things that works at eight weeks. At a year out, teaching a topic properly works. At one term out, technique installation works, because the pupil is changing how they answer rather than learning new facts. At eight weeks, timed practice with immediate correction works. At two weeks, only light practice and sleep work, and new material actively harms by displacing consolidation. Anyone offering to teach a syllabus in April is selling comfort.

faqs.question: Which subjects should be left until late in a crowded revision plan?
faqs.answer: The ones where late work is genuinely effective: biology terminology precision, Computer Science pseudocode conventions, History source technique, and English reading analysis. All four are technique rather than content, so they respond to work in the final quarter. Deal early with the subjects where content must be taught: chemistry moles, physics algebra, and literature set texts. The ordering feels wrong because it defers the subjects that sound most alarming, and it is what the calendar actually supports.

faqs.question: Does Ramadan change the revision plan for a June candidate?
faqs.answer: It changes the timing rather than the content. Where the revision quarter overlaps Ramadan, school days shorten and evenings restructure around Iftar, so sessions move to a post-Iftar slot rather than disappearing. A family that reschedules keeps the most valuable period in the two-year course intact; a family that pauses loses six weeks at precisely the point when timed practice and immediate correction are the only interventions still capable of moving a grade. Book the rescheduled slots in advance, because availability tightens from January.

faqs.question: Where should we get IB session and results dates from, if not here?
faqs.answer: Because none could be confirmed from the International Baccalaureate itself. The IB's own site returns an error to automated checking, so no IB session or results date in this project has been verified at source. Secondary sources circulate dates and they are not good enough to act on, since an examination date is something a family makes irreversible plans around. Write to your child's IB coordinator or check ibo.org directly, and treat any IB date on any tutoring page, including the ones that look authoritative, as unverified.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to Al Mushrif, Al Bateen or Al Reem Island?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service offered only in India. Tutoring for Abu Dhabi families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. In the final quarter that matters practically: a family wanting three sessions a week cannot afford one lost to a bridge delay or an island access route, and an online slot has no journey to disrupt. It also removes the travel premium inside the published AED 180-500 in-home band.

faqs.question: What should we bring to the first session to plan the calendar?
faqs.answer: Three things from the school. The board and specification code for each subject, with the tier, from the examinations officer in writing. The centre's Cambridge administrative zone. And your child's last marked script, not the report grade. With those, the remaining weeks can be planned against what actually works at that distance from the paper, rather than against the order of the textbook. The first session is free, is one session, and requires no card details.

Send the second to yourself with the live official timetable attached from the board's own site. Then work backwards from the paper: content teaching only in the autumn, technique in the spring term, timed practice with immediate correction in the last eight weeks, and nothing new in the final fortnight. A free trial lesson is one session with no card details required. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-muna-aca.tutorsIntro: The tutors below support Arabic as a first and as an additional language, and the primary and lower secondary curriculum that precedes IGCSE, one-to-one over live video. Support follows the prescribed content a school is required to deliver rather than substituting an alternative course.

intro.heading: The three subjects every international curriculum sits alongside
paragraphs: Parents at a British, American or IB curriculum school in the UAE spend a great deal of attention on the international curriculum and very little on the three subjects that run beside it, which is understandable and leaves a gap. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are not optional extras added by individual schools. They are a federal requirement: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations.

That single sentence is the foundation of everything on this page, and it explains a pattern families notice without understanding. Why a child is in a different Arabic class from the friend they sit with in mathematics. Why the language of instruction in one lesson is Arabic and in another the school's own. Why the content cannot be swapped for a tutoring provider's own materials. And why these subjects cannot be used to make up a number in one process that matters later.

The detail is set out most publicly in Dubai, where KHDA has published mandatory-subject guidelines with specific rules on streaming, language of instruction, teacher approval and time allocation, to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year and by April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. Abu Dhabi's requirements are set by its own regulator, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. So the published Dubai detail is useful as a worked illustration of how these rules operate, and an Abu Dhabi family should confirm the specifics with ADEK and their own school.

The point that reaches furthest is the equivalency one. The Ministry of Education's British-track rules require five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A family whose timetable relies on them to reach the number has not reached it, and the shortfall only becomes visible at the point of attestation. One competitor ranking for UAE tutoring queries publishes a six-subject requirement, which does not match the published rule.

This page therefore covers what the three subjects are, how streaming and language of instruction work, how time is allocated, what the equivalency exclusion means for a subject list, and the narrow limits on what any tutoring in these subjects may be. Tutoring is not required for equivalency, admission or progression, and anybody suggesting otherwise is making a false claim about a regulatory process. Tuition for Abu Dhabi families is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and home visits are a service offered only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-muna-aca.programmesIntro: The three subjects run from the earliest primary years through to the end of school, and what they demand changes at each stage. Below is how they sit alongside the international curriculum at each point.

programmes.name: Primary years
programmes.description: Where Arabic reading fluency and script accuracy are built, and where the gap between Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language widens most. Progress is measurable week to week at this age, which makes it the stage at which support is both cheapest and most visible. Social and Moral Studies content is introduced here too.
programmes.countryNote: Primary families in the UAE meet these requirements earlier than families elsewhere and usually without much explanation. Asking the school which stream a child is in, in which language the lessons are delivered, and how much weekly time each subject receives is a reasonable set of questions with factual answers.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3
programmes.description: The stage at which these subjects start competing with the international curriculum for a pupil's attention, because the secondary timetable tightens. A pupil who has coasted in Arabic through primary meets the consequence here, and the gap is harder to close against a crowded week than it was at nine.
programmes.countryNote: Where a school prepares pupils for an Arabic IGCSE entry, the decision about which route - first language or additional language - is usually taken at the options stage and reflects the stream a pupil has been in for years rather than a fresh assessment.

programmes.name: IGCSE years
programmes.description: The mandatory subjects continue regardless of the examination timetable, and in some schools an Arabic IGCSE entry exists alongside them. This is where the equivalency exclusion becomes practically relevant, because a subject list is being fixed and Arabic and Islamic Education cannot be counted towards the Ministry's five.
programmes.countryNote: UAE candidates sit the June and November series; the February/March Cambridge series is offered in India only. Any Arabic IGCSE entry sits in the same series as everything else and competes for the same revision weeks in the spring term.

programmes.name: Sixth form and the Diploma
programmes.description: The federal requirement continues in school, and separately the IB Diploma's own structure requires a language, which for some pupils is Arabic. Those are two distinct things and conflating them causes confusion: one is a national requirement and the other is a programme requirement with its own assessment.
programmes.countryNote: For MoE equivalency on the British track, the published requirement alongside the five IGCSE subjects is one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Verify the current position on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-muna-aca.subjectsIntro: The mandatory subjects first, with the streams and language rules that apply, then the international-curriculum subjects they sit alongside. Confirm the specifics for your emirate with your school and its regulator.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: For Arab pupils, with Standard Arabic required as the main language of instruction under KHDA's published Dubai guidance. A separate class from the additional-language stream, because curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ between the two.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: For non-Arab pupils, taught as a language rather than as a literature and culture course. Script accuracy, reading fluency and spoken confidence are the measurable targets, and all three move visibly at primary age.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required provision with streamed classes. KHDA's published guidance requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Arab pupils and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs, and requires teachers to hold appropriate approval to teach the subject.

subjects.name: Social Studies
subjects.description: Part of the federal baseline alongside Arabic and Islamic studies. KHDA's Dubai guidance requires Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils, with separate classes from the non-Arab provision.

subjects.name: Moral, Social and Cultural studies
subjects.description: Delivered to non-Arab pupils in the school's licensed-curriculum language under KHDA's published Dubai rules. Content is prescribed, which is why no provider may substitute its own materials for it.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge IGCSE 0580)
subjects.description: The international-curriculum subject these three sit alongside most comfortably, because the demands do not overlap. Counts towards the Ministry's five accredited subjects in a way Arabic and Islamic Education do not.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500 and 0990)
subjects.description: Where a pupil is learning to analyse language in two systems at once, which is demanding and also mutually reinforcing: the habit of asking what a word does transfers between Arabic and English work.

subjects.name: The Cambridge sciences
subjects.description: Biology 0610, Chemistry 0620 and Physics 0625, all counting towards the Ministry's five. The practical component in each is examined as written method, which is the same precision skill the mandatory subjects reward in a different language.

subjects.name: Literature in English (Cambridge 0475 and 0992)
subjects.description: Set texts chosen by the school. Worth noting for a crowded timetable that this is a subject whose content cannot be learned late, unlike several technique-led ones.

subjects.name: Humanities and Business subjects
subjects.description: History 0470, Geography 0460, Economics and Business Studies. All count towards the five, and all reward the same evaluative writing discipline that Social Studies work develops in its own language.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-muna-aca.regionsTitle: The Abu Dhabi communities this page serves
abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-muna-aca.regionsIntro: Schools in the Al Mushrif corridor draw from the established island districts and the newer villa communities. For primary-age support the fact that matters is bedtime rather than traffic, since sessions should be short and early.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Established central districts with short school runs, so children are often home by half past three. That makes a twenty-five minute Arabic session at four genuinely workable, which is the shape that suits this age.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Island districts with a concentration of established schools and short journeys. Twice-weekly short sessions are practical here, and frequency matters far more than duration for script and reading work.

regions.name: Al Nahyan and Al Mamoura
regions.note: Central and well connected, with early returns home. Families here often run two children at different stages, which makes a fixed short slot per child easier to sustain than a flexible arrangement.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Tower living where lift and parking delays would add real time to any visit. For short primary sessions that overhead is disproportionate, which is one reason the format matters more at this age than at sixteen.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island and Al Zaab
regions.note: Single-access routes that behave badly at peak, pushing an in-home start past five. A tired seven-year-old at half past five produces a weaker session than a fresh one at four, which is a real cost.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: Large villa communities with long runs and substantial internal distances. Weekend morning sessions are common here, and they work well for reading aloud and script practice.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Mussafah
regions.note: Mainland communities with awkward bridge and corridor congestion. Removing the journey entirely is what makes a twice-weekly short session possible rather than theoretical.

schoolClusters.city: The Al Mushrif and city-centre cluster
schoolClusters.note: Established primary and all-through schools serving the island districts, all delivering the mandatory subjects alongside their licensed curricula. Families here are often choosing a secondary school at the end of the primary phase, which makes the stream and language questions worth asking of both schools.

modes.description: Twenty-five to thirty minutes, twice a week, aimed at one thing: script accuracy, reading fluency, or spoken confidence. sections.heading: The federal baseline, stated exactly
paragraphs: The rule that sits underneath everything else is short. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the federal position, and it is why a British-curriculum school in Abu Dhabi, an American one in Dubai and an IB one in Sharjah all deliver the same three subject areas alongside quite different international programmes.

Enforcement and detail sit with the emirate regulators, which is where the confusion comes from. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain fall under the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai has the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

Because detail is set at emirate level, the most publicly documented version is not necessarily the one that applies to a given family. KHDA has published mandatory-subject guidelines for Dubai with specific rules on streaming, language of instruction, teacher approval and time allocation, with the requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year and April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. That document is the clearest public illustration of how these rules work in practice.

For an Abu Dhabi family, the honest position is therefore this: the federal requirement applies, the detailed rules are ADEK's, and the published Dubai guidance shows the kind of specificity these requirements carry. The practical action is to ask your own school three factual questions - which stream, which language of instruction, how much weekly time - and to confirm anything consequential with ADEK rather than with a tutoring page.

sections.heading: Two Arabic subjects, not one
paragraphs: The single most useful thing a non-Arab family can understand is that Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different subjects with different expectations, not two difficulty levels of the same course. The first-language route treats Arabic as the pupil's own language, with the literature, grammar and register expectations that implies. The additional-language route teaches Arabic as a language being acquired.

KHDA's published Dubai guidance makes the streaming explicit: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. That is not a staffing convenience or a school preference; it is a requirement with a stated reason.

It also explains something families notice and misread. A child in a different Arabic class from a close friend has not been separated by ability. The grouping follows the two distinct courses, and a parent who asks about moving their child into the other class is usually asking to change which subject they study rather than which set they sit in. Understanding that in advance prevents a frustrating conversation with a school that cannot grant the request.

For a non-Arab pupil the practical targets on the additional-language route are concrete and measurable: letter recognition and script accuracy, reading fluency aloud, vocabulary in the topics the school is covering, and spoken confidence. All four move visibly at primary age with short frequent practice, which is why this is one of the subjects where modest and well-aimed support produces the clearest results.

sections.heading: Language of instruction, and why it differs by group
paragraphs: KHDA's published Dubai guidance sets out the language of instruction precisely, and the precision is the point. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils. For non-Arab pupils, the school's licensed-curriculum language is used for Islamic Education and for Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

That arrangement means two pupils in the same year group can study the same subject area in two different languages, which is exactly what the separate-classes requirement exists to accommodate. It is not a difference in seriousness or depth; it is a recognition that a subject delivered in a pupil's own language and the same subject delivered in an acquired one are different teaching tasks with different outcomes.

There is a credential requirement attached, and it is unusually checkable. KHDA's guidance states that schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach these subjects. For a Dubai parent that is a concrete thing to ask about. For an Abu Dhabi parent the equivalent question is what ADEK requires of teachers in these subjects, which is a reasonable question to put to a school directly.

The implication for any outside support is immediate. A tutor working on Islamic Education content for an Arab pupil is working in Standard Arabic, and one working with a non-Arab pupil is working in the school's curriculum language. Those are different briefs requiring different people, and a provider who does not ask which applies before matching has not understood the requirement they are claiming to support.

sections.heading: How much time these subjects actually take
paragraphs: Time allocation is the part families are least often told and most often curious about, because it determines how much of a week the mandatory subjects occupy alongside an already full international curriculum. KHDA's published guidance states that mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on the basis of a 40-minute lesson unit, that schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and that it is advised that the length for any mandatory subject lesson is at least 25 minutes.

Those three provisions together explain a timetable that can look odd. A school meeting its weekly total with four thirty-minute lessons rather than three forty-minute ones is operating within the rules, and a school running a short daily Arabic slot is doing something deliberate rather than improvised. A parent wondering why Arabic appears at awkward points in the week is usually looking at a solution to a weekly-total constraint.

For an Abu Dhabi family the specific figures are ADEK's to set, and the useful question to the school is simply how much weekly time each mandatory subject receives and how it is distributed. That is a factual question with a factual answer, and it tells you something more useful than any general statement about how seriously a school takes these subjects.

The practical consequence for support is that these subjects are not short of taught time. A pupil struggling in Arabic is usually not struggling for lack of lessons; they are struggling because the lessons assume a base they do not have, which is a different problem and one that short frequent practice outside school addresses well. That is an argument for twenty-five minute sessions twice a week rather than for an additional hour that duplicates the school's provision.

sections.heading: The equivalency exclusion, and what it does to a subject list
paragraphs: This is the consequence that reaches furthest beyond school and the one almost nobody plans for. The Ministry of Education's published requirements for the British track specify that a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Separately they must submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade.

The detail that matters here is that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. For a pupil with a full nine or ten subject timetable this is academic, because the five are comfortably met by mathematics, English, sciences and humanities. For a pupil on a thinner timetable, or one considering dropping subjects, it is arithmetic that should be done before the subject list is fixed rather than discovered at the point of attestation.

There is a related error circulating. One competitor ranking for UAE tutoring queries states that candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published five-subject rule. A family planning a timetable on a wrong number plans badly in one direction or the other, and the fix costs nothing but a check against moe.gov.ae or the emirate attestation authority.

Two things should be said plainly alongside this. No IB points threshold for equivalency is published in the sources available here, so none is quoted on this page; that figure must be confirmed on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority before anyone relies on it. And IB Gram does not perform, process or guarantee equivalency or attestation - the process belongs to the Ministry and the emirate authority, and tutoring is not required for it.
