sections.heading: What tutoring in a mandatory subject may and may not be
paragraphs: The limits here are tighter than in any other subject and they are worth stating before any arrangement begins. KHDA's published Dubai guidance states that for the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. That is an unusually direct restriction, and it means no provider may run an alternative Arabic or Islamic Education course alongside a school's prescribed one.

What support can legitimately be is reinforcement of what the school is required to deliver. Reading aloud from the school's own material. Practising script formation. Learning the vocabulary of the topic the class is covering. Rehearsing spoken responses. Working through the exercises the pupil has been set. None of that introduces different content; all of it increases the pupil's practice with content already prescribed.

What it cannot be is a parallel curriculum, a different textbook, a provider's own scheme of work, or material imported from another country's Arabic programme because it is more convenient to teach. A provider offering any of those for a mandatory subject is offering something the rules do not allow, and a family accepting it is also accepting that the pupil is practising the wrong thing for the school's assessment.

The same restraint applies to published material generally. Cambridge, Pearson and the IB own their syllabuses, past papers and mark schemes, and the right behaviour is to link the official page rather than hand over files. And no provider holds regulator approval: IB Gram holds no ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership and makes no such claim. Describing tutors as approved to teach Arabic or Islamic Education would be a particularly serious misstatement, since that approval is a real thing schools must hold for their own staff.

sections.heading: When the real pressure is on the international curriculum
paragraphs: It is worth saying that the more common situation is the reverse of this page's subject. A family worried about Arabic is often actually looking at a pupil who is managing Arabic adequately and losing marks in mathematics or English, where the consequences for a certificate and a sixth-form application are larger. Diagnosing which is which before buying anything prevents a term of work aimed at the wrong subject.

The distinguishing question is what the report and the marked work say, separately for each subject. A pupil whose Arabic reports note script accuracy and whose mathematics reports note missing working has two problems of very different sizes: the second one affects five accredited subjects and a tier entry, and the first one affects a subject excluded from that count. That is not a reason to neglect Arabic; it is a reason to order the spending.

The international-curriculum diagnosis is also more concrete, because external instruments exist. A Cambridge or Pearson past paper from the official board site, sat under timing and marked against the published scheme, with lost marks sorted into content, method, precision and timing, tells a family exactly what is wrong. Nothing comparable exists for a school's internal Arabic assessment, where the school's own judgement is the main available evidence.

So the practical sequence for a family at a UAE primary or lower secondary school is to establish the mandatory-subject facts once - stream, language, weekly time - and then to decide whether any paid support belongs in those subjects or in the international curriculum. For most families the answer is the latter, and for some it is neither. Both are legitimate conclusions for this page to reach.

sections.heading: Coverage, permits and the first session
paragraphs: Arabic as an additional language is covered in this set and a match is usually quick. Arabic as a first language is a thinner pool, and Islamic Education support within the prescribed content is thinner again, because the brief is narrow by design. Mathematics, English and the sciences at primary, lower secondary and IGCSE level are well covered. In a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free, and that is better said than filled.

Only three answers are possible to a request from an Al Muna family, and you should be told plainly which one you have. The least welcome is that the brief is not currently covered — an Arabic first-language slot in a particular week, say, or Islamic Education within the prescribed content — and the right response to that is to name it, not to send a generalist who can read the script but cannot teach the grammar. The second is that it is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which we disclose rather than conceal behind a local-looking telephone number; the rate is the same as it would be for a tutor living in Khalidiyah, because where a person sits does not change what an hour of their teaching is worth. The third, and the usual outcome for mathematics, English and the sciences, is that the brief is covered and a trial lesson goes into the diary within days.

Parents are entitled to check the one credential that exists for an individual tutor. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website or e-services system under the service name Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, which lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Separately, ADEK's reported professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of pupils enrolled at their own school, so that arrangement should not be sought.

The first session is free, is one session, and requires no card details. The useful things to bring are a sample of your child's own work in the subject you are concerned about, and the answers to three questions from the school: which stream, which language of instruction, and how much weekly time. With those, the session can establish whether any paid work is warranted at all, and in which subject. A recommendation of none is a legitimate and frequent outcome.

At primary age the format has a specific advantage: short sessions twice a week are practical over video and awkward to arrange as visits, since nobody will drive across the island to deliver twenty-five minutes. Pupils receive substantial taught time in the mandatory subjects, so a child who is struggling is usually struggling because the lessons assume a base they do not have rather than because there are too few lessons. Where it is not, the better use of the same money is usually the international curriculum, and sometimes the answer is neither.

intro.heading: Marks do not leave a paper evenly, and the pattern is always the same
paragraphs: A grade is a number that hides a distribution. Two students with the same IGCSE Mathematics mark can have lost it in completely different places, and their next six weeks of work should look nothing alike. One has dropped a cluster of marks on bearings, bounds and similar shapes, which is a content problem in three narrow topics. The other has lost marks evenly across the whole paper on unwritten method, which is a single habit affecting everything. Same grade, opposite remedies.

Across hundreds of IGCSE and Diploma scripts the distribution is remarkably predictable. In Mathematics the recurring content clusters are bearings, upper and lower bounds, similar-shape ratios and premature rounding, with unwritten method running underneath as a tax on every structured question. In Physics it is electromagnetic induction and circuit analysis, with missing definitions costing the first mark of every explain question. In Chemistry it is units and the practical write-up. In Biology it is command terms, not content.

There is a fourth category that families almost never name and that costs more marks at IGCSE than any single topic: pacing. A candidate who leaves eight marks unattempted at the end of a paper has lost more than a candidate who misunderstood bounds, and the two are fixed in entirely different ways. Pacing is measurable in one exercise, improves over four or five full papers, and is invisible in a grade. Nobody sells tutoring for it because it is not a subject, and a student can go two full years without anyone ever timing a single question they answer.

This page therefore works at topic level. Each subject below names its recurring clusters and what a session does about them, and the tables set out the diagnosis exercises that produce the information: how to categorise a marked script, how to measure pacing, how to compare the three sciences for return on time. The competitor pages measured for this project in October 2026 do not operate at this level at all; five of six carry no table, and not one maps a topic to a paper.

Two things to state plainly. Tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, since home visits are a service offered only in India. And nothing on this page promises a grade, a score or an improvement; what it offers is a specific description of where marks go and what can be done about each kind of loss, which a parent can check against their own child's next marked paper. That is a narrower promise than most of this market makes, and it is the only kind that can be tested in six weeks rather than in August.

programmes.name: Primary, Foundation Stage to Year 6
programmes.description: The three things worth checking are automaticity in number facts, reading stamina on unfamiliar text, and whether the child can write a paragraph with a point and support without a template. A primary report can read well while one of those is missing, because teacher assessment measures the curriculum rather than the foundations the next six years will lean on. Each is cheap to fix at this stage.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3, Years 7 to 9
programmes.description: Nothing is externally examined, so nothing feels urgent, and that is why the cheapest useful tutoring in the whole market goes unbought here. The specific risk is algebraic manipulation: a Year 9 who cannot confidently rearrange a formula will meet that exact gap simultaneously in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry eighteen months later, in three subjects with three different teachers and no obvious common cause.

Counting the accredited subjects on the option sheet at this point is worth more than it sounds.

programmes.name: IGCSE, Years 10 and 11
programmes.description: Two linear years ending in terminal papers, where the losses are predictable and the diagnosis is cheap. Syllabus codes set the paper structure: Cambridge 0580 or 0980 Mathematics, 0620 Chemistry, 0625 Physics, 0610 Biology, or Pearson 4MA1, 4CH1, 4PH1, 4BI1. Tiering caps the grade available. Most of the recoverable marks in these two years are convention and pacing rather than content.

programmes.name: A Level, and the Diploma as an alternative sixth form
programmes.description: A Level narrows to three or four subjects studied in depth, and the first term exposes which IGCSE habits were actually understanding and which were procedure. Students who scored well on recall meet questions that reward applying an idea to an unfamiliar context. Some Abu Dhabi families instead move to an IB Diploma school, taking six subjects with internal assessment in each plus the Extended Essay.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-al-yasmina-.subjectsIntro: Each subject below names its recurring loss clusters at topic level. These are the things a first session should be spent on, and they are checkable against your own child's last marked paper rather than taken on trust.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 / 0980 / 4MA1)
subjects.description: Recurring content clusters: bearings, upper and lower bounds, similar-shape area and volume ratios, and values rounded that should have stayed exact. Running underneath all of them is unwritten method, which taxes every structured question on the paper. Confirm the code first, because 0580 and 0980 report on different grading scales.

subjects.name: Physics (0625 / 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electromagnetic induction and circuit analysis are the two heaviest clusters, and both improve markedly once the student draws the circuit or the field before writing anything. The separate loss is the missing stated definition: the first mark of a three-mark explain question is routinely available for a sentence the candidate never writes.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620 / 4CH1)
subjects.description: Units omitted from mole calculations are a binary loss, present or absent on the script, and therefore the fastest thing in any science to eliminate. The practical component separates candidates on whether a described method could actually be followed. Organic naming and the reactivity series are recall and can be banked a year early at a low rate.

subjects.name: Biology (0610 / 4BI1)
subjects.description: The dominant loss is answering the wrong command term, which is why a student with strong content knowledge can sit at a C. Separate a marked paper into content losses and verb losses and the split usually surprises the family. Graph interpretation and experimental design hold most of the remaining recoverable marks.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Two papers testing different skills that students revise as one subject. Reading rewards precise retrieval and inference against the clock; directed writing rewards addressing form, audience and purpose explicitly. A candidate who writes fluently but ignores the specified form loses marks that have nothing to do with the quality of the prose.

subjects.name: English Literature
subjects.description: The commonest loss is a well-informed tour of the plot where a sustained argument was required. Quotation handling is marked: short, embedded and analysed outscores long and unexamined every time. Marking essay plans rather than finished essays produces faster improvement and gives a weekly artefact instead of a fortnightly one.

subjects.name: Mathematics (A Level and AS)
subjects.description: The IGCSE habit that stops working is pattern recognition: at A Level the question is deliberately unfamiliar and the method has to be chosen rather than recalled. Algebraic fluency becomes the limiting factor rather than a convenience, and students who got away without writing method lines find that the marks for them are now a significant share.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Relevant for families moving to a Diploma sixth form. Energetics and organic mechanisms separate Higher Level grades, and data-based questions reward reading the axis labels before the question stem. The internal assessment is the most controllable set of marks in the course and the most often postponed to the deadline.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools alongside the British curriculum, and taught in a separate stream from Arabic as a first language by requirement, because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. A tutor should be matched to this stream specifically rather than to Arabic in general, since the syllabus and ceiling differ.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.description: Case study detail is the differentiator and students revise themes instead. A named example with figures and a date earns credit that a general statement cannot, and the commonest loss is an answer that could have been written about anywhere. Source evaluation in History is a technique, not an opinion, and responds quickly to a few marked attempts.

sections.heading: IGCSE Mathematics: the clusters that take the marks
paragraphs: Mathematics at IGCSE loses marks in a small number of recognisable places, and the list is short enough to be actionable. Bearings is first, because it combines angle reasoning with a convention students half-remember. Upper and lower bounds is second, and it is the topic most often taught once and never revisited. Similar shapes is third, specifically the area and volume ratios, where students apply the length ratio and lose everything that follows. Premature rounding is fourth and is purely procedural.

Underneath those sits the single largest loss in the subject, which is not a topic at all: method not written down. The mark scheme awards the working, and a candidate who performs a correct calculation mentally and records only the answer forfeits marks they had already earned. On a structured paper this recurs on almost every multi-mark question, which means it can account for more lost marks than the four content clusters combined.

The useful diagnosis exercise takes twenty minutes and a marked paper. Go through the script and sort every lost mark into one of four columns: a content cluster, unwritten method, a reading or transcription error, or marks lost to running out of time. Then count the columns. Most families find the content column is the smallest, and that single observation usually changes where the next six weeks of work go. The table sets out the exercise and what each outcome implies, and the right-hand column is deliberately specific so that the sort produces a plan rather than an observation.

sections.heading: The two English papers nobody prepares separately
paragraphs: English Language at IGCSE tests two different things and almost every student revises it as one subject. The reading component rewards precise retrieval and defensible inference under time pressure, which is a skill of reading carefully and quoting economically. The writing component rewards addressing a specified form, audience and purpose explicitly, which is a skill of planning before writing. A candidate can be strong at one and weak at the other and come out with a middling grade that explains nothing.

The commonest writing loss has nothing to do with the quality of the prose. A task that asks for a letter to a head teacher and receives a well-written essay loses form marks regardless of how good the essay is, because form is assessed. The fix is mechanical and fast: before writing anything, the student states the form, the audience and the purpose in three short phrases at the top of the page, and then writes to them. Two sessions usually install it.

The commonest reading loss is answering from impression rather than from the text. Students who annotate deliberately for the first few minutes outscore those who begin answering immediately, and the gap widens on inference questions. In English Literature the parallel loss is a tour of the plot where a sustained argument was wanted, and the fastest intervention there is marking essay plans rather than complete essays, which produces a weekly artefact and takes a fraction of the time.

sections.heading: The three sciences compared on return for time spent
paragraphs: Families with a limited budget and three weak sciences have to choose, and the honest answer is that the sciences do not respond equally fast to tutoring. Chemistry usually gives the quickest return, because a large share of its recoverable marks sit in binary conventions: units written or not written, a method followable or not followable, a named reagent correct or not. Those are fixable within a fortnight and show up immediately on the next paper.

Biology is second, because its dominant loss is command-term discipline rather than content, and that is a habit rather than a knowledge base. A student who learns to match the verb to an answer shape recovers marks across the whole paper at once. The remaining Biology losses, in graph interpretation and experimental design, take a little longer but are also technique rather than memory.

Physics is usually slowest, and that is worth saying plainly because it is the subject families most often want fixed fastest. Its heaviest clusters, induction and circuit analysis, rest on conceptual understanding that cannot be installed as a convention, and the definition problem is a memory task that takes repetition. The quick win in Physics is the definition set and the habit of drawing before writing; the rest is a term of work. The table sets out the comparison so a family can allocate deliberately rather than by anxiety. Spending the budget on the slowest-moving subject first is the commonest and most understandable allocation error in this market, because it is usually the subject causing the most distress at home.

sections.heading: Pacing: the loss that costs most and has no subject name
paragraphs: A candidate who leaves the last eight marks of a paper unattempted has lost more than a candidate who misunderstood one topic, and in most cases nobody has ever told them. Pacing does not appear on a report, does not belong to a subject, and is not what tutoring is advertised for, which is why it survives untreated through two years of a linear course and then decides a grade.

It is measurable in one exercise. The student sits a full paper under genuine timed conditions and writes the clock time in the margin at the end of each question. Afterwards, the time per question is compared with the marks available. The pattern is almost always the same: far too long on the early questions, which are worth least, and then a collapse at the end where the marks were densest. Seeing their own numbers changes a student's behaviour more than any amount of advice.

The repair takes four or five full papers rather than a session, because it is a behavioural habit under pressure rather than a piece of knowledge. The mechanism is simple: a target time per mark, a hard rule about moving on, and a deliberate decision about which question to leave. Students resist the last of those strongly, because leaving a question feels like failure, and the single most useful thing a tutor does here is make the arithmetic of that choice explicit until it stops feeling wrong.

sections.heading: A Level Mathematics and the IGCSE habits that stop working
paragraphs: The first term of A Level Mathematics is where a particular kind of strong IGCSE candidate struggles, and it is consistently misread as effort or attitude. At IGCSE the questions are recognisable: a student who has seen enough past papers can identify the type and recall the method. At A Level the question is deliberately unfamiliar, and the method must be selected from several possibilities on the basis of what the question is actually asking.

That shift exposes two IGCSE habits. The first is pattern matching instead of understanding, which works until the pattern is withheld. The second is loose algebra, which was survivable when the numbers were small and becomes the limiting factor when an expression runs to three lines. Students who got away without writing method lines also discover that method now carries a significant share of the marks rather than a token one.

The useful response is narrow and early. Six to ten sessions in the autumn term, aimed at the transition rather than the syllabus, cost substantially less than twenty sessions in the second year trying to recover a grade, and they work on exactly three things: algebraic fluency drilled to automaticity, choosing a method from the question rather than from memory, and writing a full solution that someone else could follow. The table maps the same transition across the subjects where it bites hardest. The week counts are ranges because the starting point varies: a student who already wrote full solutions at IGCSE closes the gap considerably faster than one who never had to.

sections.heading: The Khalifa City afternoon, and why the slot matters more than the rate
paragraphs: A topic-cluster repair block or a pacing programme only works if the sessions actually happen on consecutive weeks, which makes the dependability of the slot more important than the hourly rate. Khalifa City's problem is specific: traffic onto the main road builds from about half past three, so a four o'clock start that looks fine on paper fails in practice for a travelling tutor and succeeds reliably for a video session set at five.

In-home rates in this emirate are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour once travel is inside the fee, with Bestimate's survey at AED 180 to 350 and local home tutors at AED 200 to 500. Online, a qualified subject tutor sits at AED 150 to 300, Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and a named-specification specialist at AED 200 to 450 or more, TutorChase publishing AED 270. Those figures belong to the providers named and none is an IB Gram quotation.

The difference that matters for the methods on this page is not the rate but the loss rate. Families with travelling tutors commonly lose two or three sessions in a twenty-eight-session term to traffic, weather or an overrun, and a pacing programme interrupted twice stops being a programme. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. What a Khalifa City family buys here is a dependable weekly slot with a specialist matched nationally rather than locally.

sections.heading: Using the June and November series as a planning tool
paragraphs: Two series a year is a planning instrument, not just a pair of dates, and almost nobody in this market treats it that way. For a UAE Cambridge candidate the series are June and November; the February and March series is offered to India only, so it is not an option and any guidance suggesting otherwise describes another country's timetable. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November.

The planning use is this. A student who is genuinely behind in one subject in a nine-subject set can sometimes be better served by a deliberate decision about which series to sit that subject in, rather than by carrying nine subjects into the same window at an unsustainable workload. That decision belongs to the school and the family together, it has to be made before final entries close, and the evidence for it is a marked paper rather than a feeling.

The other use is the resit, and the timings matter. Backward-looking anchors are checkable: Pearson's November 2026 final International GCSE timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students the day after, and November 2025 results arrived with students on 22 January 2026. The gap between summer results and the next entry deadline is short, so the resit decision is made under time pressure. Forward windows are named by month only here, because provisional timetables are revised.

sections.heading: Coursework: what a tutor may do, and what nobody may do
paragraphs: Some specifications carry coursework or a non-examined assessment, and a sixth form carries more. In every case the submission must be the student's own work, and the consequence of a breach falls on the student rather than on anybody selling help. Setting the boundary before the first session of this kind avoids a conversation that is much harder to have halfway through a draft.

The permitted work is wide and is the service. Read the published assessment criteria alongside the student and explain exactly what each descriptor awards. Press on an investigation title or research question until it can be answered within the word limit. Teach the statistical test, the laboratory technique, the referencing convention or the model the task needs. Read a draft the student wrote and name the criterion costing marks. Rehearse the meeting the student is about to have with the teacher who marks it.

The prohibited work is simple: no contributed text, no redrafting into a final version, no data supplied for the student to present as collected, no edit that leaves the submission substantially someone else's. One operation ranking in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price, which is an academic-integrity breach and a malpractice trigger for the student rather than the seller. The test a student can apply unaided is whether they could explain every sentence of their own submission, unprompted, to the person who will mark it. If they could not, the line has already been crossed whoever crossed it, and the only honest repair is to return to the last version that was genuinely theirs.

No satisfaction percentage or star rating appears, because none can be evidenced with a sample, a date and a method.

faqs.question: Which maths topics take the most marks from an IGCSE candidate?
faqs.answer: Four content clusters recur: bearings, upper and lower bounds, similar-shape area and volume ratios, and values rounded that should have stayed exact. Underneath them sits the single largest loss in the subject, which is not a topic at all: method not written down. The mark scheme credits the working, so a candidate who calculates mentally and records only the answer forfeits marks already earned, and on a structured paper that recurs on almost every multi-mark question.

faqs.question: How do we sort a marked maths script into something useful?
faqs.answer: Sort every lost mark into one of four columns: a content cluster, unwritten method, a reading or transcription error, or marks lost to running out of time. Then count the columns. It takes about twenty minutes and most families find the content column is the smallest of the four, which is the single observation most likely to change where the next six weeks go. A mixed result with no dominant column usually points to foundation work rather than exam technique.

faqs.question: What is the pacing problem and how is it measured?
faqs.answer: It is marks left unattempted at the end of a paper, and it frequently costs more than any single topic. To measure it, the student sits a full paper under genuine timed conditions and writes the clock time in the margin after each question. Comparing time spent against marks available almost always shows the same pattern: far too long on the early, low-value questions and a collapse at the end where the marks were densest. Seeing their own numbers changes behaviour faster than advice does.

faqs.question: How long does it take to fix pacing once we know it is the problem?
faqs.answer: Four or five full papers rather than a session, because it is a behavioural habit under pressure rather than a piece of knowledge. The mechanism is a target time per mark, a hard rule about moving on, and a deliberate decision about which question to abandon. Students resist that last part strongly, since leaving a question feels like failure, and making the arithmetic of the choice explicit until it stops feeling wrong is the main thing a tutor contributes here.

faqs.question: Our child has three weak sciences and one budget. Which should we tutor?
faqs.answer: Chemistry usually gives the fastest return, because a large share of its recoverable marks sit in binary conventions: units written or not, a method followable or not, a reagent named correctly or not. Those move within a fortnight. Biology is next, because its dominant loss is command-term discipline, a habit rather than a knowledge base. Physics is slowest, since induction and circuit analysis rest on conceptual understanding that takes a term to build properly.

faqs.question: Why does our child write well in English and still score in the middle?
faqs.answer: Because form is assessed separately from quality. A task asking for a letter to a head teacher that receives a well-written essay loses form marks however good the essay is. The fix is mechanical: before writing anything, the student notes the form, the audience and the purpose in three short phrases at the top of the page and then writes to them. Two sessions usually install it, and it recovers marks that had nothing to do with the standard of the prose.

faqs.question: Is English Language one subject or two different skills?
faqs.answer: Two, and treating it as one is why preparation often fails to move the grade. The reading component rewards precise retrieval and defensible inference against the clock, which is a skill of reading carefully and quoting economically. The writing component rewards addressing a specified form, audience and purpose explicitly, which is a skill of planning before writing. A candidate strong at one and weak at the other finishes with a middling grade that explains nothing about what to do next.

faqs.question: What is the fastest fix available in IGCSE Physics?
faqs.answer: A memorised definition set, stated before any explanation. The first mark of a three-mark explain question is routinely available for a sentence the candidate never writes, and twelve definitions learned verbatim recover marks across the whole paper. Second fastest is drawing the circuit or the field before attempting the question. The slower work, in electromagnetic induction and circuit analysis, rests on conceptual understanding and realistically takes a term rather than a block.

faqs.question: Why do strong IGCSE mathematicians struggle in the first A Level term?
faqs.answer: Because IGCSE questions are recognisable and A Level questions are deliberately not. A student who has seen enough past papers can identify a question type and recall the method; at A Level the method has to be chosen from several possibilities based on what the question is actually asking. That exposes pattern matching used in place of understanding, and loose algebra that was survivable with small numbers and becomes the limiting factor across a three-line expression.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to address an algebra gap in Year 10 or Year 11?
faqs.answer: Year 10, by a wide margin. Foundation work sits at the lower market bands, roughly AED 65 to 150 an hour, because it is content teaching rather than diagnosis, and it can run as a term of short frequent practice. The same gap addressed in Year 11 costs the specialist band, competes directly with exam preparation for the available hours, and has to be patched rather than rebuilt. It is the least popular correct answer in this market.

faqs.question: Can we choose which series a subject is sat in?
faqs.answer: Partly, and it is an underused planning tool. A UAE Cambridge candidate sits the June series or the November series; the February and March series is offered to India only. A student genuinely behind in one subject within a nine-subject set is sometimes better served by a deliberate decision about which window that subject goes in, rather than carrying everything into one. The decision belongs to the school and the family together and must be made before final entries close.

faqs.question: How quickly do we have to decide on a November resit?
faqs.answer: Within weeks of summer results, which is why the decision gets made under pressure. The checkable anchors are historical: Pearson's June 2026 International GCSE results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students the day after, November 2025 results arrived with students on 22 January 2026, and the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Base the decision on the component breakdown rather than the overall grade, and get a per-subject entry quote from the centre in writing.

faqs.question: Does a travelling tutor actually matter for a six-week repair block?
faqs.answer: Yes, more than for an open-ended arrangement. Families with travelling tutors commonly lose two or three sessions in a twenty-eight-session term to traffic, weather or an overrun, and two losses turn a six-week block into nine weeks, which breaks the comparability the method depends on. Khalifa City traffic builds from about half past three, so a four o'clock start fails in practice for a driver. IB Gram does not sell home visits in the UAE at any rate.

faqs.question: What do online and in-home tutoring cost around Khalifa City?
faqs.answer: Online, a qualified subject tutor sits at AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and a named-specification specialist at AED 200 to 450 or more, with TutorChase publishing AED 270. Entry-level online rates run lower, with Tutopiya advertising from AED 33 to 52. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180 to 500 once travel is inside the fee. Every figure belongs to the provider named, not to IB Gram.

faqs.question: Can a tutor rewrite a weak coursework paragraph to show what good looks like?
faqs.answer: No, because a rewritten paragraph in the student's document is contributed text regardless of the intention behind it. What a tutor can do is explain exactly what the descriptor awards, mark the paragraph the student wrote and name what is missing, show an unrelated worked example, and let the student rewrite it themselves. One operation ranking in this market sells completed coursework outright; the thing that purchase risks is the student's qualification rather than the seller's business.

faqs.question: Which subjects count for UAE equivalency on a British-curriculum option sheet?
faqs.answer: Five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no lower than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from those five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. A page currently ranking in this market says six IGCSE subjects; the published figure is five. Count the accredited subjects at Year 9 options rather than discovering the margin at the attestation stage years later.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-aldar-acade.tutorsIntro: Matching works from three facts rather than one: the curriculum the school is licensed for, the stage the student is at, and the named assessment coming next. For a household with children at two schools in the same group, that means two separate matches rather than one compromise.

intro.heading: A group of schools is not a single curriculum, and a request has to say which
paragraphs: Most tutoring enquiries name a school and a subject. For a family at a single-curriculum school that is usually enough. For a family at one school inside a group it frequently is not, because schools within a group can run different curricula, serve different age ranges, and use different examination boards, while sharing a name, an admissions system and a reputation. A request that says only the group name and the subject gives a matcher nothing specific to work with.

The three facts that actually determine the match are straightforward to supply. First, the curriculum the particular school is licensed for, which for a group in Abu Dhabi commonly means a British-curriculum pathway, sometimes with other routes elsewhere in the group. Second, the stage: primary, lower secondary, the IGCSE years, or post-16. Third, the named assessment coming next, which might be a Cambridge or Pearson syllabus code, an internal criterion task, or a school-set examination. Those three sentences change a general enquiry into a specific one.

Verify the first fact rather than assuming it. Abu Dhabi's private schools, including those in Al Ain, are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection outcomes. The school's own site and the regulator's listing are the two places to confirm curriculum, year groups and programmes, and they should be the source rather than a tutoring page, including this one. Each school in a group is licensed individually, so a curriculum confirmed for one sibling's campus proves nothing about the other's.

The second thing a group creates is the two-board household, which is more common here than anywhere else in this market. Siblings at different schools within the same group, or one child who transferred and one who did not, produce a situation where a single household needs criterion-based support for one child and paper-based support for the other, on two calendars, with one budget. That is a scheduling and allocation problem as much as an academic one, and it has specific answers set out further down.

Two matters of fact before the detail. Tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, since home visits are a service offered only in India. And IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge or Pearson, and names no school or group on this page as a client, partner or endorser. Students supported by tutors do attend schools in the emirate; that is the whole of the relationship.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-aldar-acade.programmesIntro: The stages below are the ones a group of British-curriculum schools in this emirate typically spans. Each is described by what it assesses, because that is what determines whether a tutor is a good match rather than merely a good teacher.

programmes.name: Primary years
programmes.description: Teacher assessment against curriculum objectives, with no external examination. The three things worth checking independently are automaticity in number facts, reading stamina on unfamiliar text, and whether the child can produce a paragraph with a point and support without a scaffold. A report built on curriculum coverage can look settled while one of those is absent underneath it.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain the mandatory UAE subjects run alongside the licensed curriculum in private schools, under the federal requirement overseen by the Ministry of Education. Arabic usually carries a conventional grade earlier than other subjects, and it is where a non-Arabic-speaking household first encounters a report line it cannot interpret or act on without help.

programmes.name: Lower secondary
programmes.description: No external assessment, ending in the option choices that fix the IGCSE set. The specific risk is algebraic manipulation, because a student who cannot confidently rearrange a formula will meet exactly that gap in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry at the same time eighteen months later, with three teachers and no visible common cause. It is also the stage where a transfer between schools is least damaging.
programmes.countryNote: Option choices at this stage carry a regulatory consequence families meet much later. Ministry of Education equivalency for British-curriculum students counts five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no lower than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among those five. Counting accredited subjects on the option sheet now is cheaper than discovering the margin at attestation.

programmes.name: IGCSE years
programmes.description: Two linear years assessed by terminal examination, with syllabus codes that determine the paper set and tiers that cap the available grade. Cambridge codes look like 0580 or 0980 Mathematics, 0620 Chemistry, 0625 Physics and 0610 Biology; Pearson Edexcel equivalents are 4MA1, 4CH1, 4PH1 and 4BI1. A transfer during these two years is the most expensive move available and sometimes unavoidable.
programmes.countryNote: A Cambridge candidate in the UAE sits the June series or the November series. The February and March series is offered to India only. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November. Cambridge allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones and states that using the correct zone timetable is essential, so dates come from the examinations officer rather than any summary.

programmes.name: Post-16, A Level or the IB Diploma
programmes.description: A Level narrows to three or four subjects studied in depth with no enforced breadth. The IB Diploma takes six subjects with three at Higher Level plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity-Activity-Service, with internal assessment in every subject. Within a group, siblings may be on different routes, and the two ask genuinely different things of a student's organisation rather than their ability.
programmes.countryNote: Equivalency on the A Level route requires one accredited Advanced Level subject at no lower than grade E, or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, in addition to the five IGCSE or GCSE passes. No IB points threshold is published on this page because none could be verified against the Ministry of Education's own site, so confirm it with the Ministry or the attestation authority.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-aldar-acade.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects most often requested across a group of schools in this emirate, each described by what it assesses so that a request can name the right level and component rather than just the subject.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 / 0980 / 4MA1)
subjects.description: Confirm the code before anything else, since 0580 and 0980 report on different grading scales and past-paper boundaries do not transfer between them. Recurring content losses sit in bearings, upper and lower bounds and similar-shape ratios, with unwritten method running underneath as a tax on every structured question.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: A different paper split from Cambridge with its own formula-sheet conventions, which is exactly why a student who transfers between schools on different boards mid-course meets unfamiliar phrasing rather than unfamiliar mathematics. The commonest error after a transfer is assuming a formula is provided when it is not.

subjects.name: Physics (0625 / 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electromagnetic induction and circuit analysis are the heaviest clusters, and the quickest available gain is a memorised definition set stated before any explanation. Practical arrangements differ between centres, which makes this one of the subjects where a transfer between schools genuinely changes what the student must prepare.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620 / 4CH1)
subjects.description: Units omitted from mole calculations are a binary loss and the fastest thing in any science to eliminate. The practical component separates candidates on whether a described method could actually be followed. Content sequencing differs between schools, so a transfer can leave a real gap in one topic while duplicating another.

subjects.name: Biology (0610 / 4BI1)
subjects.description: The dominant loss is answering the wrong command term rather than missing content, which is why a knowledgeable student can sit at a C. Sorting a marked paper into content losses and verb losses usually surprises a family. Graph interpretation and experimental design carry most of the remaining recoverable marks.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IGCSE · A Level · DP HL and SL
subjects.description: Two separate skills at IGCSE that students revise as one subject: precise retrieval and inference against the clock, and addressing a specified form, audience and purpose. At Diploma level the Individual Oral usually fails on a global issue too broad to evidence in ten minutes rather than on the texts themselves.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: For students on the Diploma route within a group. Algebraic fluency carries the course, the paper without a calculator concentrates the losses, and Higher Level adds proof and complex numbers where a missing justification line costs more than an arithmetic slip. Internal assessment rewards a genuinely owned question.

subjects.name: Economics and Business
subjects.levels: IGCSE · A Level · DP HL and SL
subjects.description: Diagrams are marks in Economics, and candidates drawing from memory rather than from the question shift the wrong curve. In Business the loss is a tool applied without the organisation's own figures. At Diploma Higher Level the pre-released case study is examined material and is routinely under-prepared.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools alongside the licensed curriculum, and taught in a separate stream from Arabic as a first language by published requirement, because curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Match a tutor to this stream specifically, since the syllabus and the realistic ceiling are different.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Runs alongside the licensed curriculum. Content is prescribed, and published guidance states that using different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission is prohibited, so support means working with the school's own material rather than substituting an alternative course for it.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-aldar-acade.regionsIntro: A group spanning Abu Dhabi and Al Ain produces two quite different logistical pictures, under the same regulator. These are the communities families travel from in both.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: The mainland villa corridor with the densest concentration of secondary-age international students outside the island. Traffic onto the main road builds from about half past three, so a dependable weekly slot starts at five rather than four, which is the single most useful piece of local scheduling knowledge here.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and the inland island
regions.note: Established neighbourhoods close to several long-standing schools, with slow roads at pick-up and a mainly long-term resident population. Multi-year arrangements are common, which suits the lower-secondary foundation work that pays off across the IGCSE set.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: The western island, a mix of villas and apartments, with a high proportion of students travelling by bus from the island core. Bus timings rather than parent diaries set the earliest session, and families here frequently need slots after seven in the evening.

regions.name: Al Reem and Al Maryah
regions.note: Dense towers at the eastern end of the island with a large school-age population commuting outward in several directions. The exit onto the main crossing in the late afternoon is the slowest stretch of the day, and weekend blocks are popular for full timed papers.

regions.name: Al Ain city centre and Al Jimi
regions.note: A different pattern entirely: shorter journeys, less congestion, and a smaller pool of local specialist tutors. That last point is the one that matters, because a family in Al Ain looking for a named-component specialist is choosing from a much narrower local list than a family on Abu Dhabi island.

regions.name: Al Ain outer districts
regions.note: Communities where school transport covers long distances and specialist local tutoring is scarcest. This is where online matching changes the available choice most dramatically, since a national pool contains the specialist and a sensible driving radius in Al Ain may not contain anyone at all.

regions.name: Saadiyat and Yas Islands
regions.note: Island communities with several newer schools, where a sibling at a different school is common. Two different assessment calendars in one household is the usual reason a family needs both criterion-based and paper-based support in the same week.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi: the island and the villa corridor
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's schools split roughly between the long-established island institutions and the newer villa-corridor and island-development schools. Families move between them more often than they move emirates, and a tutor familiar with one school's examination calendar generally recognises the others.

schoolClusters.city: Al Ain and the wider emirate
schoolClusters.note: Al Ain sits under the same regulator as Abu Dhabi city but has a smaller pool of local specialist tutors, which is why online matching makes a larger practical difference there. Families here are more likely to be long-term residents planning a full secondary sequence.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-aldar-acade.modesIntro: Three arrangements, and for a two-school household the right answer is usually two of them running in parallel rather than one shared between children.

modes.title: Per-child matched arrangement
modes.description: Separate tutors and separate slots for each child, matched to each child's own curriculum, stage and next assessment. Families often resist this on cost grounds and try to find one tutor to cover both, which usually produces a compromise that serves neither. Two correctly matched half-arrangements outperform one shared full arrangement in almost every case we see.
bullets: One match per child, on that child's actual assessment

modes.title: Transfer bridging block
modes.description: A finite block of six to twelve sessions for a student who has moved between schools, boards or curricula, aimed at the gap the transfer created rather than at the subject generally. Content sequencing differs between schools, so a transfer commonly leaves one topic entirely untaught while another has been covered twice, and the first job is finding out which.
bullets: Six to twelve sessions, finite and targeted

modes.title: Shared foundation work, where it genuinely is shared
modes.description: There is one case where two children can be served by one arrangement: lower-secondary foundation skills, where the content is close enough that algebraic fluency or paragraph structure can be built in parallel. Even then the sessions are separate; what is shared is the tutor and the method, not the hour. Attempting to share an hour between two children halves both.

sections.heading: What differs between schools inside one group, and why it matters
paragraphs: A group shares a name, an admissions process and often a leadership structure, and parents reasonably infer from that a shared curriculum. Frequently the inference holds; sometimes it does not. Schools inside a group can serve different age ranges, sit in different cities under the same regulator, use different examination boards for the same subject, and sequence content differently even where the board is the same. None of that is visible from the group name.

The practical consequence is that a tutoring request has to be school-specific, not group-specific. The three facts to supply are the curriculum the particular school is licensed for, the stage the student is at, and the named assessment coming next. Where a family is unsure of the first, the school's own site and the regulator's school listing are the authoritative sources, and the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the emirate including Al Ain.

The table sets out the variables that actually change between schools in a group, with what each one means for a tutoring match. Reading it the other way round, it is also a checklist for a family considering a transfer between schools within a group: the questions in the left column are the ones to ask admissions before, not after, the move. A transfer that looks straightforward administratively, with the same uniform and the same admissions office at both ends, can still cost a student a term of unfamiliar conventions.

sections.heading: The same subject, assessed three different ways
paragraphs: Within one household it is entirely possible for Chemistry to mean three different things. For a lower-secondary student it is teacher-assessed against curriculum objectives with no external paper. For an IGCSE candidate it is a set of terminal components on a named syllabus code with a tiered grade range. For a Diploma student it is papers with published weightings plus an internal assessment marked against criteria. A tutor strong in one of those can be ineffective in another.

This is the specific reason a shared tutor across siblings so often disappoints. The tutor is not weak; the match is wrong for one of the two children. A teacher who is excellent at paper technique on a Cambridge specification may have never read an internal assessment criterion descriptor, and a tutor fluent in criterion work may have no feel for timed-paper pacing. Neither gap is a failing, but both are invisible until several sessions in.

The table sets the three assessment logics side by side with what each one actually requires of a tutor. The useful conclusion for a family is to ask a prospective tutor which of the three they work in most, and to believe the answer. A tutor who claims equal fluency in all three on all levels is making a claim that is hard to verify, and the trial lesson is the place to test it with a specific document rather than a general question. Ask for that trial on the child's own marked script, not on a sample one.

sections.heading: Transferring between schools mid-course, and what it costs
paragraphs: A transfer inside a group is administratively straightforward and academically uneven. The most expensive moment to move is during the two IGCSE years, because the course is linear, the board may differ, and content sequencing almost certainly does. A student can arrive at a new school having covered a topic the class finished last term and having never met one the class covered first, and nothing in the enrolment process surfaces that.

The first job after any mid-course transfer is therefore an audit rather than tutoring. Take the specification, go through it topic by topic, and mark each one as covered, partly covered or not met. Two conversations produce most of the answer: the subject teacher at the new school on what the class has done, and the student's own books from the previous school on what they actually studied. The gaps that emerge are specific and finite, which makes them cheap to close.

The second job is conventions, which are easier to miss than content. A move between Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel changes paper splits, formula-sheet provision and question phrasing. A move between a criterion-assessed programme and a terminal one changes everything about how work is produced and marked. The practical test is to put one past paper from each board in front of the student and watch which instructions they hesitate over. Both are learnable in a handful of sessions, and both cause a first-term dip that is routinely attributed to settling in rather than to a specific and fixable mismatch.

sections.heading: The first term after a move, and why the dip is misread
paragraphs: A student who transfers mid-course almost always dips in the first term, and the dip is usually explained as settling in. Sometimes that is right. More often it is a specific and nameable mismatch, and the difference matters because settling in resolves itself while a mismatch does not. A family that waits a term for a social explanation to resolve an academic problem has spent the cheapest available time doing nothing.

The tell is the shape of the losses. A genuine settling-in dip is broad and shallow: slightly worse across everything, improving slowly, with no single topic conspicuously absent. A mismatch dip is narrow and deep: one topic answered as though it had never been taught, because it had not, or an entire paper approached with the wrong conventions. Looking at the marked work tells a parent which they are dealing with inside twenty minutes. A report comment saying the student is still adjusting is not evidence either way, because it describes the behaviour rather than the script.

The practical sequence is short. Collect the first marked assessment from the new school. Sort the losses into content, convention, and anything that looks like genuine unfamiliarity with the task format. Compare the content losses against the audit of what the previous school actually covered. If the two line up, the problem is a sequencing gap and it is finite. If they do not, look harder at conventions before concluding that the student has suddenly become weaker at a subject they were previously fine at.

sections.heading: Two boards, one household, one budget
paragraphs: The two-school household is the characteristic situation for a family inside a group, and it creates an allocation problem rather than an academic one. Two children at different stages on different assessments need different tutors, different slots and different methods, while the family has one budget and one set of evenings. Trying to resolve that by finding one tutor for both is the commonest mistake and the most understandable one.

The arithmetic actually favours separation. Two correctly matched arrangements at a shorter frequency usually outperform one shared arrangement at a longer frequency, because a session aimed at the wrong assessment produces very little regardless of its length. A fortnightly session with a tutor who knows the right mark scheme beats a weekly session with one who does not, and for a family with a fixed monthly figure that is the trade worth making. Set the monthly figure first and then decide how to split it, rather than pricing each child separately and discovering the total afterwards.

The second part of the allocation is which child to prioritise, and the honest answer is the one closer to a terminal assessment with marks at stake. A Year 11 candidate twelve weeks from a June series has a harder deadline than a Year 8, and the Year 8 work is cheaper to buy later while the Year 11 work is not. Saying that plainly to both children, with the reason, tends to work better than pretending the allocation is equal when it is not.

sections.heading: Abu Dhabi and Al Ain: one regulator, two different markets
paragraphs: Schools in Al Ain sit under the same authority as those in Abu Dhabi city. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the emirate, so the inspection framework, the vocabulary of the ratings and the complaints route are identical in both. Guidance written for a Dubai audience points families in either city at the wrong regulator, and across the competitor pages measured for this project in October 2026, ADEK was named by nobody at all.

What differs sharply between the two cities is the tutoring market rather than the regulation. Abu Dhabi island and the villa corridor hold a comparatively deep pool of local tutors, including people with marking experience on specific specifications. Al Ain's pool is smaller, which means a family seeking a specialist in a named component may find that no realistic driving radius contains one. That is a structural feature of a smaller city rather than a criticism of it.

This is where online delivery changes the available choice most, and it is worth being concrete about why. The argument is not convenience. It is that a national pool contains a tutor who has marked Pearson 4PH1 Paper 1 or coached a Diploma internal assessment to a high band, and a sensible radius in Al Ain may contain nobody who has done either. In-home rates across the emirate are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour once travel is in the fee; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, since home visits are a service offered only in India.

sections.heading: Two calendars that do not line up, and how to plan around them
paragraphs: A household with children on different programmes is managing two assessment calendars that peak at different moments, and the overlap is where the stress accumulates. The IGCSE candidate's pressure points are the final entry deadline months before the paper, the mock window in the preceding term, and the series itself. The Diploma student's pressure points are internal: five internal assessment deadlines and a four-thousand-word Extended Essay converging in one stretch of the second year.

The calendar facts worth fixing are specific. A Cambridge candidate in the UAE sits the June series or the November series; the February and March series is offered to India only, and guidance suggesting a spring sitting describes another country's timetable. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that using the correct zone version of the timetable is essential, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after using the wrong one.

For the Diploma side, no session or results date appears on this page, because none could be verified from the International Baccalaureate's own site, which returns an error to automated checking. Dates must come from the school's Diploma coordinator. Backward-looking anchors on the Cambridge and Pearson side are checkable and worth keeping: the November 2026 Pearson final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students the day after, and November 2025 results arrived with students on 22 January 2026.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when one tutor works with two children
paragraphs: A shared tutor across siblings raises a question that does not arise with a single child, and it is worth naming. Work produced for one child's assessment must not reach the other's, and a tutor who has coached one student's internal assessment or coursework on a topic should be careful about how they handle an overlapping piece from the sibling. The obligation sits with the tutor, but a family that is aware of it is less likely to create the situation accidentally.

The general boundary applies in both cases and is the real service. A tutor can read the published criteria with the student and explain what each descriptor awards. They can press on a research question or investigation title until it is answerable within the limit. They can teach the statistical test, the laboratory technique, the referencing convention or the model the task requires. They can read a draft the student wrote and name the criterion costing marks. They can rehearse the supervisor or teacher conversation.

What is never permitted is contributing to the submission: no text, no redraft into a final version, no data presented as collected, and nothing carried across from a sibling's work. One operation ranking in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price, which is an academic-integrity breach and a malpractice trigger for the student rather than the seller. The self-test each student can apply alone is whether they could explain every sentence of their own submission, unprompted, to the person who will mark it.
