sections.heading: Coverage, VAT and the first session
paragraphs: Mathematics, the sciences and the essay subjects at both Cambridge and Pearson tiers are well covered in this set and a match is usually quick. Thinner briefs exist: Computer Science 0478 with pseudocode conventions, Additional Mathematics 0606, Arabic as a first language, and unusual literature text lists. In a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free, and that is better said than filled with a generalist at any band.

Three outcomes are possible and a family should be told which applies. The brief is covered and a trial lesson is scheduled within days. The brief is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which is disclosed rather than concealed behind a local-looking telephone number - and that disclosure matters, because two ranking competitors route UAE parents to numbers outside the country without saying so. Or the brief is not currently covered, in which case it is named.

On tax, this page states nothing about the UAE VAT treatment of tuition fees, because doing so would require a Federal Tax Authority citation and the position turns on a provider's own registration and the nature of the service. What a family can reasonably require is a quoted AED figure with a plain statement of whether VAT is included, excluded or not applicable, plus a tax registration number where one is held. A provider who will not put that in writing has answered a different question.

The first session is small by design. A free trial lesson is one session, with no card details required, and the useful thing to bring is your child's last marked paper rather than a description of the problem. Within that hour it should be possible to name the job - coverage, habit, diagnosis, stretch or scarcity - and therefore the band that fits it. If the answer is that the floor of the market would serve your child perfectly well, that is a legitimate thing for this page to have told you.

process.title: Name the job before asking the price
process.description: Content coverage, habit installation, script diagnosis, top-end stretch, or a scarce specification. Each has a band attached, and naming the job first prevents both common errors: paying specialist rates for coverage, and buying coverage when diagnosis was what was needed.

process.title: Ask two questions at every band
process.description: Which specification code and tier is my child entered for, and what are the components? And, having read this marked script, how many marks went to method as against content? A tutor who answers both concretely is worth their rate. One who answers in general terms is a floor-level service, whatever they charge.

process.title: Ask to see the MoHRE permit
process.description: It was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Because it is free, anyone citing licensing costs in their rate has misread their own paperwork. And do not arrange tutoring with your child's own class teacher.

process.title: Consider a hybrid rather than one band
process.description: Group content coverage at around AED 100 to 150 per pupil, plus a small number of one-to-one diagnostic hours at the specialist band at the start and before the series. That buys the thing a group cannot do without paying specialist rates for the thing it can. Nobody packages it this way; assemble it yourself.

process.title: Price the journey separately
process.description: In Abu Dhabi the in-home premium is mostly distance: corridor runs to Al Reef and Al Shamkha, internal distances inside Khalifa City and Al Raha, single access routes on and off the islands. Decide whether an adult in the room is worth that, and remember it also narrows the tutor pool to whoever lives nearby.

whyPoints.title: The market read bottom-up, with sources
whyPoints.description: Every band is attributed to the provider or survey that published it and presented from the cheapest upwards, so each step has to justify itself. Three of the highest-ranking pages in this market publish no price at all and two quote in US dollars, which is not a currency an Abu Dhabi family transacts in.

whyPoints.title: The job matched to the band
whyPoints.description: Content coverage, habit installation, script diagnosis, stretch and scarcity are five different jobs with five different prices. Naming which one you need prevents paying for diagnostic capability nobody will use, and prevents buying coverage when diagnosis was the requirement.

whyPoints.title: ADEK named and explained
whyPoints.description: Abu Dhabi's regulator appears on none of the researched competitor pages. Its professional-ethics position on teachers tutoring their own pupils is set out here with the caveat that press reports should be verified against the current policy document, because the practical advice does not depend on the exact wording.

whyPoints.title: Only verifiable claims made
whyPoints.description: The MoHRE permit, the specification code, a sixth form's published entry grades and the market bands are all checkable, and the page says where. Satisfaction percentages, star ratings and proportion-reaching-top-grades claims are not checkable in this market and are not made here.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and coverage stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are an India-only service. Where a specialist is working from outside the UAE that is disclosed rather than hidden behind a local-looking number, and the rate does not change.

whyPoints.title: No regulator or board affiliation
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership and claims none. It has no office or centre in Abu Dhabi, and its tutors should never be described as regulator-approved.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest realistic rate for an Amity International School Abu Dhabi pupil?
faqs.answer: Around AED 33 to 65 an hour online, which is a real floor rather than a loss-leader: Tutopiya advertises from roughly AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, both drawing largely on university students and overseas graduates. Those rates are genuinely good value for Key Stage 3 fluency work, for Core-tier content coverage, and for a pupil who needs competent company rather than diagnosis. What they do not reliably deliver is an Extended-tier script marked against a published mark scheme with the lost marks categorised.

faqs.question: What does paying AED 150 instead of AED 50 actually buy?
faqs.answer: Specification knowledge. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and the Bestimate survey puts qualified subject tutors at AED 150 to 300. The difference is a trained teacher who has taught the syllabus rather than someone who studied the subject, which shows in knowing what a mark scheme awards and why. For Extended-tier work that is the sensible default. For a Year 8 pupil who needs arithmetic drilled to fluency, it buys capability nobody in the arrangement will use.

faqs.question: When is the AED 200-450 specialist band worth paying?
faqs.answer: In four situations. Extended-tier script diagnosis, where a marked timed paper has to be read and the losses categorised. Top-end stretch, where a pupil at a 7 is chasing the genuinely demanding marks above it. A scarce specification such as Computer Science 0478 with pseudocode conventions or Arabic as a first language, where the rate reflects supply. And a specific Diploma internal assessment brief, where scoring a draft against lettered criteria requires familiarity with them. Outside those four, the mid band is usually sufficient.

faqs.question: What is left to buy above the specialist band, at AED 500 and beyond?
faqs.answer: Scarcity and reputation, which is a legitimate thing to charge for and not the same as evidence of effect. BartyED advertises AED 650 for a named premium tutor. The honest point is that nothing in this market is measured: not one of the researched providers publishes outcome data with a sample size, a date and a stated method, and several carry satisfaction percentages and self-asserted star ratings with nothing checkable behind them. A rate above the specialist band is a claim about positioning, and a family paying it should know that is what it is.

faqs.question: Can a teacher from my child's own Abu Dhabi school tutor them privately?
faqs.answer: It is the one arrangement in this market that is explicitly discouraged, and you should not pursue it. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct is also reported to bar serving students affiliated with their own school. Those reports should be verified against the current ADEK policy document, but the practical advice holds either way.

faqs.question: What is ADEK and why does no other tutoring page mention it?
faqs.answer: The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi, as the emirate's regulator. It appears on none of the researched competitor pages, which is a striking omission on pages aimed at Abu Dhabi families. For comparison, Dubai's regulator is KHDA, Sharjah's is SPEA, Ras Al Khaimah has a Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Naming a regulator is not the same as being approved by one, and no provider should imply otherwise.

faqs.question: Does a tutor in Abu Dhabi need a licence, and does it cost anything?
faqs.answer: A permit, and it costs nothing. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. MoHRE's service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the smart app, website or e-services system. Because it is free, a provider citing licensing costs in its rate has misread its own paperwork. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: Are the fines for unlicensed tutoring really AED 50,000?
faqs.answer: No amount can be verified, so do not act on any figure circulating online. The official position is that individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. Press reporting has noted that the ministry did not specify the fine amounts or detail the penalties, so a specific number repeated on tutoring pages is not sourced. The practical point for a parent is simply to ask to see the permit, which is free to hold and quick to obtain.

faqs.question: Is a group class in Abu Dhabi good value?
faqs.answer: For content coverage, yes. Small-group rates in this market run around AED 100 to 150 per pupil against AED 200 to 450 for one-to-one specialist work, and the social element helps some pupils work. What a group cannot do is diagnose, because a session pitched to a group addresses the average gap rather than your child's specific pattern of lost marks. Ask whether individual timed scripts are marked between sessions; often they are not. A hybrid of group coverage plus a few diagnostic hours is usually the best value available.

faqs.question: Why is in-home tutoring more expensive in Abu Dhabi than it looks?
faqs.answer: Distance, in three forms. A corridor run out to Al Reef or Al Shamkha is a substantial round trip. Villa communities like Khalifa City and Al Raha have internal distances that add time after the arrival. And Yas and Saadiyat have single access routes that behave badly at peak. The published AED 180 to 500 in-home band is priced against exactly those journeys. The hidden second cost is selection: an in-home tutor must live nearby, so a family often gets a generalist rather than the right specialist.

faqs.question: How can I tell whether a tutor really knows the specification?
faqs.answer: Two questions, asked at any rate. Which specification code and tier is my child entered for, and what are the components? And, having read this marked script, how many marks went to method as against content? A tutor who answers both concretely has read the syllabus and the script, and is worth whatever they charge. A tutor who answers in general terms about building confidence is providing a floor-level service and should be priced as one, however impressive the profile.

faqs.question: Should we expect VAT on top of the hourly figure we were quoted?
faqs.answer: Ask the provider to state it in writing before the first invoice. This page does not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition fees, because that would require a Federal Tax Authority citation and the position depends on the provider's own registration and the nature of the service. What a family can reasonably require is a quoted AED figure with a plain statement of whether VAT is included, excluded or not applicable, plus a tax registration number where one is held. A provider who avoids the question in writing has answered a different one.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to Khalifa City, Al Reef or Yas Island?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service offered only in India. Tutoring for Abu Dhabi families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. The cost consequence is direct: the travel priced into the published AED 180 to 500 in-home band is not in the figure at all, and the tutor is chosen for the specification and tier rather than for living within a drivable radius of your community.

faqs.question: What if the tutor is not based in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Then that is disclosed, and the rate does not change. The published band for the subject and tier is what applies whether a specialist is working from inside the UAE or into Gulf Standard Time from outside it. Disclosure matters here because two ranking competitors route UAE parents to telephone numbers outside the country without saying so, and one shows a Dubai footer address on an Abu Dhabi page. A family is entitled to know where the person teaching their child actually is before the first session.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-amity-inter.closingHeading: Name the job, then read the bands upwards
abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-amity-inter.closingBody: Decide first which job you are buying: content coverage, habit installation, script diagnosis, top-end stretch, or a scarce specification. Then read the published bands on this page from AED 45 upwards and stop at the first one that can do that job. A free trial lesson is one session with no card details required. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.tutorsIntro: These tutors work to named specifications and components rather than to year groups, which is what a school running GCSE into a sixth form needs. A request naming a paper reaches someone who has marked that paper rather than someone who has taught the subject generally.

intro.heading: Hourly rates are how tutoring is sold; monthly totals are how it is paid
paragraphs: An hourly rate tells a parent almost nothing. AED 250 an hour sounds manageable until it is two subjects twice a week, at which point it is AED 4,000 a month and a conversation at the kitchen table. This page therefore starts where the family actually starts: the monthly figure, with the session count attached so the number means something.

The monthly packages visible in this market give the shape. Around AED 799 a month buys eight online sessions from a budget provider. In-home packages advertise at roughly AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour visits, which is the same total hours at double the price, with the difference being the driving. The Bestimate rate survey for the 2026-27 year puts monthly estimates for a single weekly one-hour session at AED 240 to 600 for budget tutoring, AED 600 to 1,200 for mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and upward for specialist exam-year support.

Underneath those monthlies sit the hourly bands, which are worth knowing so a quote can be checked. Online, a university-student tutor sits around AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor online runs AED 150 to 300, Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. A named-specification specialist is AED 200 to 450 and above, TutorChase publishing AED 270. The highest published figure in the market is BartyED's AED 650. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180 to 500 once travel is inside the fee.

Each of those numbers belongs to the provider named beside it, not to IB Gram, and none of them is a quotation. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. Lessons for Abu Dhabi families are delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which is why the monthly comparison in the first table below is not a like-for-like swap of one delivery method for another.

The reason the monthly view matters more than the hourly one at Brighton College specifically is the shape of the school year. A British-curriculum school running GCSE into a sixth form produces two expensive stretches: the spring of Year 11 and the autumn of the final sixth-form year. A family that budgets an average across twelve months and then meets both peaks at full rate is the family that stops tutoring in April, which is the worst possible month to stop. The whole point of converting hourly rates into monthly ones is to see that peak coming from September rather than from April, when the only remaining choices are to pay the top of the band or to go without.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.programmesIntro: Brighton College Abu Dhabi runs a British-curriculum pathway, so the three stages that carry a tutoring budget are the GCSE and IGCSE years, the sixth form, and the lower secondary years that quietly determine both. Each has a different monthly profile.

programmes.name: Lower secondary, Years 7 to 9
programmes.description: No external examination, which makes this the cheapest stage to fix anything and the easiest to postpone. One session a month at the budget band is often enough, which is AED 65 to 150 and not a budget item at all. The skills that decide GCSE grades are set here: rearranging a formula, structuring a written argument, and the habit of writing method lines down.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi these years also carry the mandatory UAE subjects, which run in private schools alongside the licensed curriculum under the federal requirement overseen by the Ministry of Education. Arabic is the usual budget surprise for an expatriate family, because it is frequently the one subject on the report card where a parent cannot usefully help at home and therefore the one that becomes a paid line.

programmes.name: GCSE and IGCSE, Years 10 and 11
programmes.description: Two linear years with terminal examinations and syllabus codes that decide the paper set. Budget peaks in the spring of Year 11, when families typically move from one weekly session to two or three a week in the weakest subjects. That shift from AED 600 a month to AED 2,500 a month is the single largest step change in a British-curriculum education budget, and it is entirely predictable a year in advance.
programmes.countryNote: The GCSE set is also a regulatory document in the UAE. Ministry of Education equivalency for British-curriculum students counts five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no lower than grade E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic Education from that count. One page ranking in this market tells parents the figure is six subjects; it is five, and budgeting a sixth subject's tutoring on a wrong number is a real cost.

programmes.name: Sixth form, Years 12 and 13
programmes.description: Three or four subjects in depth, where the step up from GCSE is steepest in Mathematics and the sciences. Monthly spend here is usually lower in total than Year 11 but concentrated in one or two subjects at the specialist rate, so the per-hour figure is higher while the hour count is lower. The autumn of the final year carries coursework or research deadlines that come as a separate block rather than a weekly line.
programmes.countryNote: Equivalency on the Advanced Level route requires one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no lower than grade E, or two accredited Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, in addition to the five GCSE or IGCSE passes. Abu Dhabi families most often discover this at the attestation stage rather than the option stage, which is late enough to be a problem rather than a decision.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme, where a family chooses it
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity-Activity-Service. The Diploma budget profile differs from A Level in one important way: internal assessment in every subject means a coursework block rather than a single one, and those blocks overlap. Families commonly underestimate the second year for exactly this reason. UAE candidates sit the May session.
programmes.countryNote: No IB points threshold for Ministry of Education equivalency is published here, because none could be verified against the Ministry's own site, and repeating an unverified figure across hundreds of pages is a liability rather than a service. Confirm the current requirement with the Ministry or the emirate's attestation authority before planning a sixth-form route around any number.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects that carry most of the tutoring budget at a British-curriculum school in this emirate, with the component where the marks actually go. The subject barely moves the rate; the level and the month of the year do.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 / 0980 / 4MA1)
subjects.description: The largest single budget line in most households, because it underpins the sciences as well as itself. Extended losses cluster in bearings, bounds, similar-shape ratios and premature rounding. A Core entry caps the grade at C, which is a ceiling set by the school at entry rather than by the exam.

subjects.name: Physics (0625 / 4PH1)
subjects.description: Definitions carry more marks than calculations. A student who cannot state what a field is in a sentence loses the three marks for the explanation that follows. Circuits and electromagnetic induction are the heaviest losses, and drawing the circuit before writing anything is the cheapest fix available.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620 / 4CH1)
subjects.description: Mole calculations written without units lose marks the arithmetic had already earned. The practical paper separates candidates sharply because it rewards a procedure somebody could actually follow. Organic naming and the reactivity series are pure recall and can be banked months early at the budget rate.

subjects.name: Biology (0610 / 4BI1)
subjects.description: Revised as a memory test, assessed on command terms. Describe, explain, compare and suggest each want a different answer shape, and a well-learned paragraph scores two out of five when the verb asked for a mechanism. Graph interpretation and experimental design are the two recoverable areas.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IGCSE · A Level · DP HL and SL
subjects.description: The unseen analysis is decided in the reading. Students who annotate for five minutes before writing consistently outscore those who begin immediately. At A Level and Diploma level the extended essay-style answer fails on structure rather than content, which is a teachable fix in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic fluency carries it. Higher Level adds proof, complex numbers and a longer calculus reach, and the non-calculator paper concentrates the damage. The commonest avoidable loss is a correct method never written down, because the mark scheme credits the working and the student recorded only the answer.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.levels: A Level · DP HL and SL
subjects.description: Diagrams are marks, and candidates drawing from memory instead of from the question shift the wrong curve. At Higher Level, Paper 3 is quantitative and is the clearest separator between a five and a seven. At A Level the equivalent is the evaluation paragraph most candidates run out of time to write.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Business Management
subjects.levels: IGCSE · A Level · DP HL and SL
subjects.description: Marks are lost applying a tool without the organisation's actual figures. At Diploma Higher Level the pre-released case study is under-prepared because students treat it as background rather than as examined material. The internal assessment needs real organisational data and a question narrow enough to answer in the word limit.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools alongside the licensed curriculum. Dubai's regulator publishes the most detailed guidance and requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. The non-Arab stream is the one usually tutored in expatriate households and has its own realistic ceiling.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.regionsIntro: The communities Brighton College Abu Dhabi families travel from, with the detail that affects a session time rather than a session price. Where you live changes the logistics; it does not change the rate.

regions.name: Bloom Gardens and Al Salam Street
regions.note: Walled villa communities close to the Al Salam Street corridor, with short school runs and heavy traffic on the surrounding roads at the end of the working day. A five o'clock session start is more reliable here than a four o'clock one, which matters when a weekly slot is held for a term.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Established island neighbourhoods with several long-standing schools nearby and a high proportion of long-term resident families rather than short postings. Demand here leans towards multi-year arrangements, which is the pattern where a fixed weekly slot pays off most clearly in monthly terms.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense residential towers with a large school-age population commuting outward in several directions. The exit onto the main crossing in the late afternoon is the slow part of the day, and families here most often ask for the latest practical weekday slot.

regions.name: Corniche and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Apartment living on the island's western edge, with students typically travelling by bus. The bus timetable, not a parent's diary, sets the earliest possible session, and that pushes weekday arrangements later than families expect when they first ask.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: The mainland villa corridor, roughly half an hour from the Al Salam Street area outside peak and considerably more inside it. For families who moved outward and kept the school place, this crossing is exactly what a travelling tutor prices into an in-home monthly package.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland residential area with a mixed school profile and longer average commutes. Households here are the most likely to run two children at two schools on two timetables, which makes a shared weekly arrangement harder to schedule and a video slot considerably easier.

regions.name: Yas Island and Saadiyat Island

modes.title: The standing weekly session
modes.description: One session a week in the same slot across a term, at AED 600 to 1,200 a month in the mid-market band. This is the lowest cost per mark gained because none of the hour is spent rediscovering where the student is. For Years 7 to 10 it is usually the only line a family needs, and keeping it running through the quiet terms is what prevents the Year 11 spike.

sections.heading: The monthly figure, with the session count attached
paragraphs: A monthly package price is meaningless without the number of sessions inside it, which is exactly how the figure gets used to mislead. AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 a month for four two-hour in-home visits contain the same eight hours of teaching. One costs twice the other, and the difference is the driving, not the teaching.

The table below converts the Abu Dhabi hourly bands into monthly totals at the session frequencies families actually buy. The in-home row is included because it is the comparison every parent makes, not because it is available here: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, and home visits are offered only in India. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

Read the right-hand column, because that is the one that catches people out. A monthly figure set in October is not the monthly figure in April. The same arrangement at the same hourly rate costs two or three times more in exam term, purely because the session count goes up. Budgeting the annual average and meeting the peak at full rate is the mechanism by which families stop paying for tutoring in exactly the month it matters most. The sensible approach is to budget the standing autumn figure as the baseline and hold the difference between that and the exam-term peak aside from September, treating it as a known cost with a known date rather than as an unpleasant surprise in the spring.

sections.heading: Three ways a tutoring bill quietly doubles
paragraphs: The first is subject creep. A family starts with maths, adds physics because the same tutor offered it, then adds chemistry because the mock went badly. Three subjects at one session a week is three times the bill and often less than three times the benefit, because attention is finite and the weakest subject never gets the concentrated work it needed. The disciplined version is to fix one subject properly and only then consider a second.

The second is the late booking premium. Specialist availability in the eight to ten weeks before a series is the scarcest thing in this market, and scarcity sets the price. A family arranging an exam-term specialist in September pays mid-band and chooses from a real list. The same family arranging it in April pays the top of the band and takes whoever remains. That premium is entirely avoidable and costs nothing to avoid.

The third is session length arbitrage running the wrong way. A sixty-minute session loses its first ten minutes to reconnecting with where the student was, so four sixty-minute sessions contain less working time than three ninety-minute ones at a similar total cost. Families who shorten sessions to control the monthly figure usually end up paying more per unit of progress, which is the opposite of what they intended. If the monthly number genuinely has to come down, cut the number of tutored subjects rather than the length of the sessions, because a ninety-minute session in one subject does more than two forty-five-minute sessions across two.

sections.heading: What a GCSE year costs against what a sixth-form year costs
paragraphs: These two years are priced differently and most families assume the sixth form is the expensive one. Usually it is not. Year 11 carries more subjects, a wider spread of weakness, and the heaviest exam-term step up, so its total is typically higher even though its hourly rate is lower. The sixth form carries fewer subjects at a higher rate, plus a coursework block that arrives as a one-off.

The practical consequence is where to put the money. In Year 11 the efficient spend is a standing weekly session in the two weakest subjects from the start of the year, which keeps the spring step up to a manageable multiple. In the sixth form the efficient spend is a specialist in the single subject that decides a university offer, plus a finite coursework block timed to the school's own deadlines rather than to a term.

The table sets both years out side by side with indicative monthly bands. Every figure is a market band rather than a quotation, and the specialist rows assume the online one-to-one rates earlier on this page. None of them is an IB Gram price; IB Gram's own terms are set in a consultation after the free trial lesson rather than published as a rate card. The one line families most often leave out entirely is the coursework block in the final post-16 year, which is finite but substantial and does not appear anywhere in a monthly average built from the autumn figures.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go, subject by subject
paragraphs: Tutoring is worth its monthly figure only if the hour attacks something specific. The losses at this level are remarkably consistent, which is why a tutor who has marked a given specification can predict them from a single script. This section names them so a parent can judge whether a session plan is addressing the real problem or restating the syllabus.

The pattern across all of them is the same: students lose marks on the shape of the answer, not on the knowledge. A candidate who can describe diffusion accurately still drops three marks when the command term was explain. A candidate who calculates a mole correctly still drops one for omitting the unit. Those are not knowledge gaps and no amount of re-teaching content closes them.

That distinction is what separates the AED 150 band from the AED 65 band in practice. Diagnosing an answer-shape problem requires reading what the student actually wrote against the mark scheme that actually applies. It cannot be done from a textbook, and it cannot be done by a tutor who has not seen that specification's examiner commentary. The table names the recurring loss per subject, which is the thing to ask a prospective tutor about in the trial lesson. If they cannot name one from a marked script in front of them, the arrangement will be content revision at a diagnostic price, and that is the single worst purchase available in this market.

sections.heading: Online delivery and the Al Salam Street commute
paragraphs: In-home tutoring in Abu Dhabi carries a travel cost whether or not the invoice shows it. A tutor reaching the Bloom Gardens and Al Salam Street area at five in the afternoon spends a substantial part of their evening on the road, and that is why the local in-home band reaches AED 500 an hour against AED 150 to 450 online. It is not a quality premium. It is a driving premium.

There is a second cost in reliability. A session that depends on a journey can fail for reasons unrelated to teaching, and across a twenty-eight-session term families with travelling tutors commonly lose two or three sessions to traffic, weather or a tutor's own overrun. In exam term those are the least replaceable hours in the year, which makes the loss worse than its proportion suggests.

The third cost is the one that decides the argument for a sixth-form candidate. Travel limits the tutor pool to whoever drives to this part of the island at that time. For a specific component such as Economics Paper 3 or a particular Physics specification, that radius may simply contain nobody with the right experience. Online delivery is not sold here as convenience; it is sold as access to a tutor who would otherwise be unreachable. In a subject where qualified teachers are genuinely scarce in this emirate, that access is the difference between the right tutor and the available one, and no monthly figure compensates for the second.

sections.heading: The GCSE to sixth-form gap, and the budget nobody sets for it
paragraphs: The step from GCSE to A Level or to the Diploma is the single most under-budgeted transition in a British-curriculum education. Students who scored a 7 or an A at GCSE on memory and neat work meet a different kind of question in the first term of the sixth form, and the drop that follows is misread as a motivation problem rather than a skills problem. It is a skills problem and it is fixable in weeks rather than terms.

What changes is the question, not the content. GCSE rewards recall and correct procedure. A Level and Higher Level reward applying an idea to an unfamiliar context, and that is a different cognitive act that nobody taught. In Mathematics the specific gap is algebraic fluency under pressure; in the sciences it is quantitative reasoning from first principles; in the essay subjects it is sustaining a line of argument rather than covering the topic.

Budget for it in the autumn of the first sixth-form year, not the spring. Six to ten sessions at that point, aimed squarely at the transition rather than at the syllabus, is cheaper and more effective than twenty sessions in the second year trying to recover a grade. The table maps the gap subject by subject with an honest estimate of the support usually needed. Those week counts are deliberately ranges, because the starting point varies: a student who wrote method lines at GCSE closes the maths gap faster than one who got away without them.

sections.heading: The November series, and what using it actually costs
paragraphs: Across the competitor pages measured for this project in October 2026, the word November returned no hits at all, meaning not one of them told a parent when their child's second attempt falls or what it costs. Cambridge International candidates in the UAE sit the June series and the November series. The February and March series exists but is offered to India only, so it is not an option for an Abu Dhabi candidate. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November.

The dates worth citing are the ones that have already happened, because those can be checked. Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students the following day. November 2025 results arrived with students on 22 January 2026. Future windows are named by month only here, since provisional timetables are revised and a pinned future date makes a page wrong without anyone touching it.

The cost of using a resit series is three things, and only one of them is tutoring. There is the entry fee, which for a private candidate is set by the examination centre rather than by the board and must be quoted per subject. There is the gap between results and the next entry deadline, which is short enough that a decision has to be made quickly. And there is a compressed tutoring block in a period when specialists are also preparing other candidates. Cambridge also allocates centres to one of six administrative zones and states that using the correct zone timetable is essential, so work from the centre's own version.

sections.heading: What a tutor will not do with coursework, at any price
paragraphs: A sixth form produces work that has to be the student's own: an internal assessment, an extended essay, a non-examined assessment. The rules are the board's and the school's, and the consequence of breaching them lands on the student rather than on anyone selling a service. This section states the boundary in advance so no coursework session starts with it unclear.

The permitted work is substantial and worth paying for. A tutor can read the published criteria with the student and explain what each descriptor awards. They can press on a research question until it is answerable inside the word limit. They can teach the statistical test, the laboratory technique or the model the piece requires. They can read a draft the student wrote and name the criterion costing marks. They can rehearse the supervisor conversation.

The prohibited work is simple to describe. No contributed text, no redrafting into a final version, no supplied data presented as collected, no editing that leaves the submission substantially someone else's. One operation ranking in this market sells completed internal assessments at a published price, and the thing that purchase risks is the student's whole qualification. The test a student can apply without help is whether they could explain every sentence of their own submission to their supervisor unprompted. If the answer is no, the line has been crossed regardless of who crossed it, and the correct response is to go back to the last point where it was genuinely their work and continue from there.

process.title: Give us the monthly number you can actually spend
process.description: Most enquiries start with a subject. Start with the budget instead and we can tell you honestly what it buys: a standing weekly session, a short specialist block, or lower-secondary catch-up at the entry band. A plan built to a real monthly figure survives the spring; one built to an aspiration does not.

process.title: Name the specification and the component
process.description: A request that says Chemistry gets a generalist. One that says Cambridge 0620 Extended, Paper 4, currently a C reaches someone who has marked that paper. The school's examinations officer holds the specification code, and it is the single most useful thing to ask them for before enquiring anywhere.

A tutor who can do that is worth the mid band; one who restates the syllabus is not, and you have spent an hour finding out rather than a term.

process.title: Get the exam-term step up agreed in advance
process.description: The spring increase is predictable, so agree the session count and the monthly figure for it in the autumn while choice still exists. This costs nothing extra per hour and removes the late-booking premium, which is the most avoidable cost in this market.

process.title: Ask what happens if nobody is available
process.description: If no specialist in that component is free when you need it, you are told before committing, with the alternatives named: a different slot, a different tutor, or a specialist outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. A family that plans for it keeps tutoring through April; a family that averages across twelve months is the one that stops in the month it matters.

whyPoints.description: A tutor allocated to a named specification and paper knows the mark scheme, the examiner commentary and the recurring loss. That is a different service from good subject teaching, and it is the service the mid and specialist bands are actually selling.

faqs.question: What should we budget per month for tutoring at a British-curriculum school in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: For one weekly session, the Bestimate rate survey for 2026-27 puts monthly estimates at AED 240 to 600 at budget rates, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Local packages include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. Those are market figures from the providers named, not IB Gram prices. The monthly total is set by session count far more than by the hourly rate.

faqs.question: Why do two monthly packages with the same hours cost twice as much?
faqs.answer: Because one includes a journey. An AED 799 monthly package for eight online sessions and an AED 1,599 package for four two-hour in-home visits contain the same eight hours of teaching. The difference is the driving, which in this emirate means thirty to forty-five minutes each way at peak and is inside the fee whether the invoice itemises it or not. IB Gram does not sell home visits in the UAE at any price; the comparison is published so a family can see what the extra money buys.

faqs.question: Which school year is the most expensive for tutoring, Year 11 or the sixth form?
faqs.answer: Usually Year 11, which surprises most families. Year 11 carries more subjects, a wider spread of weakness and the heaviest exam-term increase, so its annual total is typically higher even though the hourly rate is lower. The sixth form carries fewer subjects at a higher rate plus a coursework block that arrives as a one-off. The efficient spend differs too: weekly sessions in two weak subjects for Year 11, a single specialist for the subject that decides a university offer post-16.

faqs.question: How much does a tutoring bill go up in exam term, and can that be avoided?
faqs.answer: The step up is roughly threefold in the mid band, as a family moves from one weekly session to two or three a week for six to ten weeks. That is not avoidable if the student needs the hours, but the late-booking premium is. Arranging exam-term support in the autumn costs the same per hour and offers a real choice of tutor. Arranging it in April means paying the top of the band and taking whoever remains, which is the most avoidable cost in this market.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to tutor three subjects at once or one subject properly?
faqs.answer: One subject properly, almost always. Three subjects at one weekly session each is three times the monthly bill and usually less than three times the benefit, because the weakest subject never gets the concentrated work it actually needed. Subject creep is the commonest way a tutoring budget doubles without the grades moving. The disciplined approach is to fix the weakest subject until the marked scripts show it, then consider adding a second, which also keeps the monthly figure predictable.

faqs.question: Are shorter sessions a sensible way to control the monthly cost?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A sixty-minute session loses roughly its first ten minutes to reconnecting with where the student was, so four sixty-minute sessions contain less actual working time than three ninety-minute ones at a similar total. Families who shorten sessions to manage the monthly figure often pay more per unit of progress than they did before. If the budget has to come down, reduce the number of tutored subjects rather than the length of each session.

faqs.question: What does the step from GCSE to A Level or the Diploma actually cost to bridge?
faqs.answer: Six to ten sessions in the autumn of the first post-16 year, which at mid-market rates is roughly AED 900 to 3,000 once. That is substantially cheaper than twenty sessions in the second year trying to recover a grade, and it is the most under-budgeted transition in a British-curriculum education. What changes at post-16 is the question rather than the content: recall and correct procedure stop being enough, and applying an idea to an unfamiliar context starts carrying the marks.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge series can an Abu Dhabi candidate sit?
faqs.answer: June and November. Cambridge International's February and March series is offered to India only, so any guidance pointing an Abu Dhabi family at a spring sitting describes a different country's timetable. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that using the correct zone version of the timetable is essential, so ask the school's examinations officer which zone applies before planning around published dates.

faqs.question: What does it cost to use the November series as a resit?
faqs.answer: Three things, only one of which is tutoring. Entry fees for a private candidate are set by the examination centre per subject and must be quoted by the centre rather than the board. Any enquiry about results carries a board fee, which the centre will state. Then there is a compressed preparation block of two or three sessions a week at AED 150 to 450 an hour. The timing is tight: November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, so the decision window after summer results is short.

faqs.question: How do we know whether a tutor is worth the mid band rather than the entry band?
faqs.answer: Ask them, in the free trial lesson, to name the recurring loss on your child's last marked script. A tutor working at the mid band or above should be able to say something specific: units omitted in mole calculations, no definition stated before an explanation, the wrong curve shifted on a diagram. A tutor who answers by describing the syllabus is an entry-band tutor regardless of what they charge, and an hour is a cheap way to find that out.

faqs.question: Does the tutor need a UAE permit to teach a Brighton College student?
faqs.answer: An individual providing private lessons in the UAE needs a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications go through the MoHRE smart app and e-services system. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published.

faqs.question: Can we pay a teacher from the school directly for evening sessions?
faqs.answer: In Abu Dhabi that is specifically restricted. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. This is press-reported rather than quoted from the policy document, so verify the wording with ADEK directly. The practical reading is that it is a compliance problem for the teacher, not a convenient arrangement for the family.

faqs.question: Will a tutor help with a non-examined assessment or an internal assessment?
faqs.answer: With the student's own draft, yes, and with the writing, no. A tutor can read the published criteria alongside the student, narrow the research question, teach the method the piece requires, mark the draft the student wrote and name the criterion costing marks, and rehearse the supervisor meeting. A tutor cannot contribute text, redraft a passage into its final form or supply data. One operation ranking in this market sells completed internal assessments, and what that purchase risks is the student's whole qualification.

faqs.question: How many GCSE or IGCSE subjects does UAE equivalency actually require?
faqs.answer: Five. Ministry of Education equivalency for British-curriculum students counts five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no lower than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among those five. There is also a post-16 requirement: one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above, or two at Advanced Subsidiary at the same grade. A page currently ranking in this market states the figure as six subjects; it is five, and budgeting an extra subject on a wrong number is a real cost.

faqs.question: Does the regulator in Abu Dhabi publish anything useful about our school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Abu Dhabi's private schools are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. Read them on ADEK's own site rather than on an aggregator, because aggregated ratings go stale and band vocabulary differs between emirates. Dubai sits with KHDA, Sharjah with SPEA, Ras Al Khaimah with its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah with the federal Ministry of Education.

faqs.question: Can a weekly slot survive Ramadan and the school holidays without extra cost?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is the practical case for video delivery rather than a selling point. During Ramadan, session timings commonly shift to after Iftar, which a video slot does by changing a calendar entry rather than a driving route. Over school holidays a family can pause the arrangement or keep it running at a reduced frequency, and a student travelling for a fortnight keeps the slot instead of losing a month of momentum. None of that attracts a rescheduling premium in an online arrangement.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.closingBody: If your child is at Brighton College Abu Dhabi, the most useful opening message gives us three things: the monthly amount you can actually commit, the specification code and component that is losing marks, and the realistic window in the week after the school run. You will get an honest answer about what that budget buys, whether a specialist in that component is free at that time, and a free trial lesson with the proposed tutor before anything is charged. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and the plan is set against the entry and submission deadlines rather than the school term.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE across mathematics, the sciences and the essay subjects, one-to-one over live video into Gulf Standard Time. Selection starts from the specification code and tier on your child's entry, not from who happens to live within driving distance.

intro.heading: The problem is arithmetic, not preference
paragraphs: Al Ain families approach tutoring with a reasonable instinct and run into an unreasonable constraint. The instinct is that a tutor in the room is better, or at least more reassuring, than a tutor on a screen. The constraint is supply. Al Ain is a smaller market than Abu Dhabi city or Dubai, and the number of people in it who specialise in Extended-tier Chemistry 0620, or Cambridge pseudocode conventions, or a specific Pearson literature anthology, and who are also willing to drive to Zakher on a Tuesday evening, is small.

When that number reaches zero, which it frequently does for a specific brief, something has to give. In practice what gives is the specialism, not the arrangement. A family that insists on a visit ends up with whoever is available and local, which means a generalist teaching a specification they have not taught, charged at the in-home premium of AED 180 to 500 an hour because the journey is real whether or not the expertise is. That is the worst value combination available in this market and it is produced by a preference rather than a decision.

The honest alternative is to accept a screen and gain the specialist, and then to compensate deliberately for what the screen removes. Because something is removed. An adult in the room has presence, which keeps a thirteen-year-old at the table. An adult in the room sees a pupil's body language when they do not understand. These are real and they matter more for younger pupils than for sixteen-year-olds.

What replaces them is evidence, produced deliberately and held by the family. Five artefacts do most of the work: the pupil's own marked script with annotations, the written mark count by category, the piece of work produced between sessions, the shared-screen record of what was corrected, and the monthly note in the school's own vocabulary. None of those exists automatically. All of them can be required at the start, and together they give a parent considerably more visibility than sitting in the next room during an in-home lesson ever did.

So this page is about that trade: what the distance costs, what replaces it, and how an Al Ain family checks that the replacement is actually happening. It also covers the regulator position, because ADEK governs private schools in Al Ain as well as in Abu Dhabi city, and its professional-ethics rules affect one arrangement families in a thin market might reasonably think convenient and should not pursue. Tuition for Al Ain families is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Al Ain or anywhere else in the UAE, and home visits are a service offered only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.programmesIntro: The presence question changes with age, and so does the evidence that compensates for its absence. Below is how the trade looks at each stage.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3
programmes.description: The stage where presence matters most, because an eleven-year-old will not keep themselves at a table. The compensation is structure rather than evidence: short sessions, the pupil working rather than listening, and an adult in the house even if not in the room. Sessions of twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week work far better than an hour.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain schools set and stream in most cases, and the set a pupil occupies at the end of Year 9 often informs the IGCSE tier a department later proposes. In a smaller market, a school's subject sets can be small enough that a pupil has no peer working at their level, which is precisely when one-to-one work earns its cost.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: The stage where the specialist matters more than the presence, and where the evidence artefacts do the most work. The highest-value activity - annotating a marked script together and re-answering the questions where marks were lost - is a shared-screen task by nature rather than a kitchen-table one.
programmes.countryNote: UAE candidates sit the June and November series; the February/March series is offered in India only. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Internal assessment work is almost entirely document-based: a draft, criterion-by-criterion feedback, a redraft. Nothing in that loop benefits from a tutor being physically present, and everything in it benefits from a specialist who knows what criterion B wants in that particular subject. The scarcity is in the criteria knowledge, not the geography.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain has a smaller Diploma cohort than Abu Dhabi city, which makes criteria-specific specialists locally scarce in a way that is purely a function of market size rather than of anything about the schools.

programmes.name: International A Level
programmes.description: The thinnest local pool of all, because depth in one subject at one specification is scarce everywhere and scarcer in a smaller market. This is the stage at which the Al Ain arithmetic is most stark: a family insisting on a local visit for A Level Further Mathematics is usually choosing between a generalist and nobody.
programmes.countryNote: Sixth forms publish IGCSE entry grades for their A Level courses and apply them, often with a mathematics requirement attached for the sciences. Those thresholds are worth looking up in Year 10 wherever a family lives, because the evidence that could change a tier entry has to exist before the entry closes.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-for-brighton-co.subjectsIntro: Each subject below carries a note on how thin the local pool tends to be, because that is the practical fact an Al Ain family needs rather than a statement about difficulty.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge IGCSE 0580)
subjects.description: The best-supplied subject anywhere, and the one where a local in-home arrangement is most likely to be genuinely available in Al Ain. Even here, Extended-tier script marking is a narrower skill than general maths teaching.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: Well supplied in general; locally the constraint is finding someone who knows this specification rather than the Cambridge one, since the calculator rules and paper structure differ.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge IGCSE 0625)
subjects.description: A thinner pool at Extended tier, and thinner again locally. The practical component is examined as written method, which makes it fully workable on a shared screen and a sensible first purchase.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge IGCSE 0620)
subjects.description: Moles and organic chemistry are the paid-for topics and the ones a generalist handles least well. This is the clearest case where a specialist on a screen beats a generalist in the room.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge IGCSE 0610)
subjects.description: The most locally available of the three sciences and the most self-remediable, since much of the gap is content volume. Terminology marking is what genuinely needs a second reader.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500 and 0990)
subjects.description: Reasonably supplied, but the work is marking the pupil's own writing against the assessment objectives, which is a narrower skill than teaching English and not evenly distributed.

subjects.name: Literature in English (Cambridge 0475 and 0992)
subjects.description: The set text list narrows the pool sharply, and in a smaller market an unusual text can empty it locally. Establish the school's list before assuming anything about availability.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge IGCSE 0478)
subjects.description: Genuinely scarce, particularly for Cambridge pseudocode conventions as against general programming. This is the subject where an Al Ain family insisting on a local visit is most likely to find nobody at all.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Scarce everywhere and very scarce locally. Where a school offers it, the bridging value into A Level or Higher Level mathematics is substantial, which makes the scarcity worth working around.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first or additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory provision alongside any international curriculum under the federal baseline for UAE private schools. Al Ain has a strong local base at additional-language level and a thinner one for first-language IGCSE entries.

sections.heading: Al Ain's tutor market, and the arithmetic of a thin pool
paragraphs: Market size determines what is available, and Al Ain is a smaller market than Abu Dhabi city or Dubai. That has nothing to do with the quality of its schools and everything to do with how many people live within driving distance who happen to hold a particular specialism. The number of local tutors who can teach Extended-tier Chemistry 0620 and mark a script against the published scheme is not large. For Cambridge Computer Science 0478 with pseudocode conventions, or Additional Mathematics 0606, it may be zero in a given month.

What happens when it is zero is the part nobody discusses. The brief does not disappear; the specialism does. A family holding out for an in-home arrangement is offered somebody local and general, often a confident graduate or a teacher of an adjacent subject, and the session becomes content coverage rather than diagnosis. The rate does not fall to match, because the published in-home band of AED 180 to 500 an hour is priced against the journey rather than the expertise.

That is the worst value combination in the market: a premium paid for travel, attached to a service that is not what was wanted. And it is entirely invisible, because a generalist going through a textbook with a competent pupil looks exactly like tutoring. The grade does not move, nobody can say why, and the explanation is usually attributed to the pupil rather than to a matching decision taken months earlier for geographic reasons.

The alternative trade is explicit. Give up presence, keep the specialism, and compensate with evidence. A pupil in Zakher can work with a specialist in Extended-tier Chemistry who would never be available to drive there, at the published online band rather than the in-home one, with every session producing a document the family can inspect. The table sets out how the pool looks across the common briefs so a family can see where the trade is real and where it is marginal.

sections.heading: What presence actually provides, and what it does not
paragraphs: It is worth being honest about the losses rather than dismissing them, because a family that has been told there are no trade-offs stops trusting the rest. An adult in the room provides presence, which keeps a younger pupil at the table when they would otherwise drift. It provides immediate reading of body language, so confusion is caught before it is admitted. And it provides a social obligation to engage that a screen weakens.

Those three things are worth most at eleven and least at seventeen. A Year 7 pupil who will not sit down without supervision genuinely benefits from somebody in the room, and for that pupil the honest answer may be that a local generalist in person beats a distant specialist on screen, because the binding constraint is attention rather than expertise. That is a real case and it should be said.

By Year 10 or 11 the balance inverts. The binding constraint becomes whether the person can tell a pupil why a six-mark explanation question scored three, and that is specification knowledge rather than presence. A sixteen-year-old does not need company; they need somebody who has marked that paper. And the activity that moves marks most - annotating their own script and re-answering the question - works better on a shared screen than on a kitchen table, because both people see the same annotated document and the pupil keeps it.

There are also things a screen provides that presence does not, and they are rarely listed. The session can be scheduled fifteen minutes after the pupil is actually home rather than after a journey. It cannot be cancelled by traffic. The marked work is shared digitally rather than carried in a bag. And the pool from which the tutor was chosen was the whole specialism rather than a drivable radius, which is the whole argument in one sentence.

sections.heading: Five artefacts that replace being in the next room
paragraphs: A parent sitting in the next room during an in-home lesson has less information than they think. They hear tone and engagement, which is reassuring, and they learn nothing about whether marks are moving. The substitute for presence is not more reassurance; it is documents. Five of them do almost all the work, and each one can be required from the first session rather than requested later.

The first is the annotated script: the pupil's own marked paper, worked through on a shared screen with notes added, saved and shared. The second is the mark count by category - content, method, arithmetic or selection, precision, timing - written down with a date. The third is the piece of work produced between sessions, which proves the arrangement extends beyond the hour. The fourth is the re-answered question, which proves the correction was acted on rather than merely explained.

The fifth is the monthly note, and it is the one that makes the others usable. Written in the school's own vocabulary - working-at grade, named component, marks on question types - it is readable by a head of department in two minutes. That matters in a smaller market where a family may want to raise a set or tier question with a school that knows them well, and where a document in the department's own language carries further than a parent's impression.

All five belong to the family. An arrangement where the evidence lives in the tutor's notes cannot be checked by the person paying for it, and that is usually not accidental. Ask for the lot at the first session, not at the twelfth. A provider who will not maintain them has told you how the arrangement will be assessed later, and it will not be with anything you can look at.

sections.heading: What an annotation session actually looks like
paragraphs: Families who have not seen one imagine a lecture delivered through a webcam, which is a fair description of a bad session and nothing like a good one. A good session opens the pupil's own marked paper on a shared screen. The tutor asks the pupil to read question seven aloud and say what they thought it wanted. Then the mark scheme is opened beside it, and the gap between the two is examined rather than explained.

The pupil then rewrites the answer, on screen, while the tutor marks it clause by clause: this earned a mark, this did not, this would have if it had named the quantity. The pupil rewrites again. That loop is the entire method and it is where marks actually move, because the pupil ends with a skill rather than a note. Three or four questions handled that way is a full hour and it is more productive than any amount of topic revision.

What makes this better on a screen than at a table is shared annotation. Both people are looking at the same document, the marks and comments are typed rather than scrawled, and the file is saved. A pupil who has six annotated scripts from a term has a revision resource built from their own errors, which is the single most useful thing a candidate can have in the final quarter and which almost nobody possesses.

The pupil also has to be able to say what happened. At the end of a session they should be able to state, in their own words, what they are doing differently next time: writing the method even when the answer is visible, naming the effect on a reader, attaching the unit. If they cannot, the session was a lecture. That check costs a parent thirty seconds and it is the most reliable quality control available at a distance.

sections.heading: ADEK governs Al Ain, and what that means for an arrangement
paragraphs: Al Ain sits under the same regulator as Abu Dhabi city. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, which includes Al Ain. That is worth stating because ADEK appears on none of the researched competitor tutoring pages, and because the regulator map across the UAE is genuinely confusing: Dubai has KHDA, Sharjah has SPEA, Ras Al Khaimah has a Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

The part with direct consequences is professional ethics. ADEK's rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct is also reported to bar serving students affiliated with their own school. Those reports should be verified against the current ADEK policy document before being quoted as its exact wording.

This matters more in a smaller market than in a large one, and that is the Al Ain-specific point. Where the local pool is thin, the most obviously qualified person who knows your child's specification and your child is frequently one of their own teachers. That is exactly the arrangement discouraged by both an emirate regulator and a federal permit's code of conduct, and it should not be pursued however convenient and well-intentioned it looks.

None of this gives any provider standing to claim regulatory approval. A page may name a regulator and explain what it does; it may not imply endorsement. IB Gram holds no ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership and makes no such claim. It has no office or centre in Al Ain, in Abu Dhabi, or anywhere else in the UAE, and its tutors should never be described as regulator-approved.

sections.heading: Distances in and around Al Ain, priced
paragraphs: Al Ain's geography is the root of everything on this page. The city covers a large area at low density, with residential districts spread from Hili in the north to Zakher in the south and school clusters distributed between them. A cross-city journey is genuinely long, and within villa districts the internal distances add further time after arrival. None of that is a complaint; it is why the in-home band exists.

Priced out, a typical in-home arrangement looks like this. A tutor travelling across the city for a 5pm session spends perhaps forty minutes each way, so a one-hour lesson is a two-and-a-half-hour commitment. Across a thirteen-week term that is roughly nineteen hours of travel inside thirteen hours of teaching. The published in-home band of AED 180 to 500 an hour reflects that ratio rather than any difference in the teaching itself.

Some families consider a tutor commuting from Abu Dhabi city, which is around ninety minutes each way. No rate makes that sustainable as a weekly arrangement, and the ones that are offered tend to collapse after a few weeks or become fortnightly, which breaks the frequency that makes tutoring work. It is the clearest illustration available of why distance and specialism cannot both be optimised in a market this size.

There is a third cost that families discover rather than anticipate: cancellation. A tutor delayed on a long cross-city or inter-city run either arrives late and teaches a short lesson, or cancels. Over a term that is money spent on nothing, and the replacement slot competes with work that has already moved. In the eight to twelve weeks before the June series, when a family may want two or three sessions a week, losing even two is material.

sections.heading: Small subject sets, and why that cuts both ways
paragraphs: Al Ain's schools are good and its cohorts are smaller, which has a specific academic consequence worth naming. A smaller year group produces smaller subject sets, and a smaller set means a pupil at the top or the bottom of it may have no peer working at their level. A pupil taking a minority subject or sitting at an unusual tier can effectively be taught in a group of one without the resource of one-to-one attention.

That cuts in the pupil's favour in one way: in a small set a teacher knows a pupil's work extremely well, and the information available at a parents' evening is often more detailed than in a large urban school. The questions that produce facts - which component is costing marks, what the method-against-content split was on the mock, what one thing the pupil should practise - tend to get precise answers here.

It cuts against them in another. A pupil whose needs sit away from the middle of a small set gets less differentiated attention, not because of any failing but because differentiation is harder with fewer pupils to group. And where a subject is offered to a handful of pupils, the school may not run the route a particular child would benefit from, including Additional Mathematics 0606 or all three separate sciences.

The practical response is to use the school's detailed knowledge and supply the differentiation separately. Ask the subject teacher for the precise brief - they will usually have one - and then get that brief worked on by someone with the specialism, wherever they happen to be. That combination uses the strength of a smaller market and works around its constraint, which is a better plan than trying to solve both locally.
