sections.heading: Internal deadlines against external deadlines
paragraphs: Families plan around examination dates and are caught by the deadlines that are not examination dates. Almost every date that actually constrains a student in Al Karamah is set by the school rather than by the board, and it falls earlier than the board's own.

The pattern is consistent. A board sets a date by which a school must upload or submit work. The school then sets its own internal deadline weeks earlier, so that it has time to check authenticity, complete marking and handle anything that goes wrong. From a student's point of view the school's date is the real one, and it is the date nobody writes on the kitchen calendar because it arrives by email in a sentence halfway down a letter.

The consequences of missing an internal deadline are also different from missing an external one. An external deadline missed can mean a component not submitted and a grade affected. An internal deadline missed usually means the student loses the feedback round, which is the thing that would have improved the piece. A draft submitted a fortnight late may still reach the board on time and will reach it unimproved, which is a quieter and more common loss.

For examination entries the same structure applies: the board publishes a final entry date and the school's examinations officer works to an earlier internal cut-off. Cambridge's zone system adds a further trap, because every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version, and Cambridge warns that it is essential to use the correct version and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. The school holds the right version; a timetable downloaded at home may not be it.

sections.heading: What a mock is for, and what it is not
paragraphs: Mock results in January and February drive most of the tutoring enquiries from central Abu Dhabi island, and they are routinely misread in both directions. A mock is a diagnostic instrument. It is not a prediction, and it is not a verdict.

The most common misreading is treating a low mock as a forecast. In several subjects the mock is sat on content the course has not finished teaching. Physics at Higher Level frequently leaves capacitance and parts of the later syllabus until the spring; mathematics at Higher Level often reaches Paper 3 material last. A student who scores poorly on a paper covering material they have not been taught has learned nothing about their ability and a great deal about the timetable. Ask which topics were examined and which have been taught before drawing any conclusion.

The second misreading is treating a decent mock as proof that nothing needs doing. Mocks are often marked generously, sometimes deliberately, to maintain confidence. They may also be a shortened paper or a reduced topic range. A comfortable mock on a restricted paper is not evidence of readiness for a full one under real timing.

What a mock is genuinely good for is a marked script. The script shows where the marks went: method not shown, rounding, misread command terms, timing collapse in the last third, and specific topic failures. That list is the only thing worth acting on, and it is worth more than the grade printed at the top. If the school does not return scripts, ask for them, because the grade without the script is a number with no instructions attached.

sections.heading: Revision timetables that survive a UAE term
paragraphs: Every Al Karamah household has made a revision timetable at some point and watched it disintegrate within a fortnight. The failure is usually structural rather than a matter of discipline, and three design faults account for most of it.

The first is scheduling by subject rather than by weakness. A timetable that gives each of nine subjects an equal weekly slot ignores the fact that some are secure and some are not, and it burns time on comfortable revision because comfortable revision feels productive. The fix is to allocate by the marked script: the clusters where marks are being lost get the hours, and secure topics get a brief retrieval check rather than a full session.

The second is planning for the week that does not exist. A timetable built on five free evenings collapses on contact with a sports fixture, a long bus run, a mandatory-subject homework load and a Thursday that nobody can work on. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside the licensed curriculum, so the homework volume is higher than the examination subject list suggests. Build the timetable on three realistic evenings and a weekend morning, and it survives.

The third is ignoring the shape of the UAE year. Ramadan shortens school days and shifts energy to the hours after Iftar; Eid removes days; the winter break removes weeks. A twelve-week revision plan in this country routinely contains eight or nine usable weeks. Counting in sessions rather than calendar weeks, and deciding in advance which weeks are skipped, keeps the plan honest and keeps the eight-session review comparing equal amounts of work.

sections.heading: The two-year Diploma calendar against the two-year IGCSE calendar
paragraphs: Side by side, the two programmes distribute their pressure in almost opposite ways, and understanding that is what lets a family support both children without either being neglected.

The IGCSE calendar is a ramp. Content accumulates through Year 10 and the first half of Year 11, then revision dominates until a single terminal series resolves everything in a few weeks. The decisive invisible moment is the tier entry, usually set in Year 10. Because the pressure is visible and concentrated, families respond to it. The risk is over-reacting late and under-reacting early.

The Diploma calendar is a series of plateaus with deadlines on them. DP1 has no external examination, which makes it feel unpressured and makes it the year most quietly wasted. Internal assessment across six subjects, the Extended Essay and the TOK components all have school deadlines, and they cluster in the first half of DP2. The examination window then arrives after most of the internal work is already submitted and unchangeable. Because the pressure is distributed and partly invisible, families under-react in DP1 and then find DP2 arrives with everything due at once.

The practical consequence for an Al Karamah household with one child in each is to treat the Year 11 series as the fixed point and the DP1 internal assessment as the thing that must be protected from it. Nothing in DP1 is urgent and several things in it are important, which is the hardest combination for any family to act on. Booking the Exploration or investigation block in the autumn of DP1 is the single decision that prevents the DP2 pile-up.

sections.heading: After the papers: results, enquiries and the resit route
paragraphs: The calendar does not end with the last paper, and the weeks afterwards contain decisions with their own deadlines. Al Karamah families are frequently caught by how long the tail is and by how short the window for acting on a result turns out to be.

The tail between sitting and receiving a result is substantial. As backward-looking illustrations from Pearson Edexcel International GCSE: June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For Cambridge, check the live official timetable for the current series. For the IB Diploma, confirm the results date with your school's IB coordinator, since we publish no IB dates.

Each board operates a process for enquiries about results, usually with a deadline shortly after results day, submitted through the school's examinations officer rather than by a parent directly. The window is short, which means a family uncertain about a grade needs to raise it immediately rather than after a fortnight of discussion. Ask the school on results day what the deadline is and what evidence an enquiry requires.

Then the resit decision. For UAE candidates a Cambridge resit points at the November series, and an Edexcel resit at November as well, which produces a result in the following January. Whether that timing works depends entirely on what the grade is needed for. A sixth-form place starting in September cannot wait for a January result; a university application the following year can. That is a calendar calculation rather than an academic one, and it is worth doing before committing to a resit rather than afterwards.

sections.heading: Ramadan planned rather than survived
paragraphs: Ramadan is the single largest predictable disruption to a tutoring plan in the UAE, and it is treated as a surprise every year. School days shorten, the working rhythm shifts, and the household's usable energy moves to the hours after Iftar. A six o'clock session that worked perfectly in January becomes the worst hour available.

There are two workable responses and one that fails. The first workable response is to move the slot into the post-Iftar window, which for many Al Karamah families is genuinely better than anything in a normal term: the house is awake, the school day was short, and the homework backlog from a full timetable is lighter. The second is to pause for the month entirely and resume afterwards, with the skipped sessions counted out of the block so nobody is paying for teaching that did not happen. What fails is keeping the original time and hoping, which produces a fortnight of missed sessions and then a conversation about commitment that is really a conversation about scheduling.

The decision should be made before the month starts, not during it. That means agreeing in advance that the slot is movable, which is a two-minute conversation when a block is set up and a difficult one once sessions have already been missed. It also means deciding what happens to the measure: an eight-session block that spans Ramadan should still be reviewed at session eight, whenever that falls, rather than at a calendar date that no longer corresponds to eight sessions of teaching.

Where Ramadan falls relative to a series matters too. In some years it sits well before the examination window and in others uncomfortably close to it, and a revision plan that assumed a normal March will need rebuilding. The sensible approach is to look at the actual term dates your school has published, count the usable teaching weeks between now and the papers, and build the plan on that number rather than on a generic twelve weeks.

process.title: Tell us the month and what has already happened
process.description: Which term, which mocks have been sat, which internal deadlines have passed, and which series the student is entered for. That is what determines whether support can still change content or only technique, and it is the information a quote without context quietly ignores.

process.title: Sit a diagnostic against the right paper
process.description: A timed paper from the correct board and tier, marked against the published scheme, with losses sorted by cause. If the student has a mock script, bring that instead and ask the school which topics it covered and which have actually been taught.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: One session at no cost and with no card required, built around the diagnostic. You leave with a written list of causes and a realistic statement of what the remaining weeks can achieve. If the match is wrong we rematch rather than persuade.

process.title: Count the sessions, not the weeks
process.description: Agree the number of sessions in the block and which weeks will be skipped for Ramadan, Eid, school closures or the series itself. A twelve-week plan in the UAE often contains eight or nine usable weeks, and counting in sessions keeps both sides honest.

process.title: Review at session eight and decide
process.description: Repeat the diagnostic, compare the two scripts, then continue, change focus, change tutor, or finish. Finishing is a real option and we will name it. A stalled plan found at session eight costs far less than one discovered in the week before the papers.

whyPoints.title: The plan starts from the calendar
whyPoints.description: September buys content, March buys technique, and the two are not substitutes. We will tell you which one the remaining weeks can actually deliver rather than quoting the same plan regardless of the month, which is what a generic offer does.

whyPoints.title: Eight weeks described honestly
whyPoints.description: Eight to twelve hours of teaching closes one diagnosed gap and rebuilds examination technique. It does not teach two years of untaught content, and nobody can promise a grade. Stating the ceiling at the start is what makes the plan trustworthy.

whyPoints.title: Internal deadlines treated as the real ones
whyPoints.description: The dates that constrain a student are the school's, set weeks before the board's. We build internal assessment blocks around the school's deadline, because a draft that arrives on time to the board and late to the teacher has lost its feedback round.

whyPoints.title: Mocks read as diagnosis
whyPoints.description: A low mock on content the course has not finished teaching is information about the timetable, not about your child. We ask which topics were examined and which have been taught before building anything on the result.

whyPoints.title: Sessions counted, not weeks
whyPoints.description: Ramadan, Eid and school closures remove teaching weeks from every twelve-week block in this country. Blocks are counted in sessions with the skipped weeks agreed in advance, so the review compares equal amounts of teaching.

whyPoints.title: Dates only where they can be checked
whyPoints.description: Cambridge and Pearson dates here carry their source and are backward-looking where they are specific. No IB session or results date is published, because ibo.org blocks automated verification. IB Gram claims no accreditation or partnership from any board or regulator.

faqs.question: We are eight weeks from the papers. Is there any point starting now?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, with an honest scope. Eight weeks at one session a week is eight to twelve hours of teaching, which is enough to close one diagnosed content cluster and re-test it, and enough to rebuild examination technique across a subject the student broadly knows. That second category matters, because most students lose a meaningful number of marks to process rather than ignorance. What it cannot do is teach content never covered, and we would say so before taking a booking rather than in week three.

faqs.question: Our son's January mock was poor. Does that predict his final grade?
faqs.answer: Not reliably, and the first question to ask the school is which topics the mock covered and which have actually been taught. Several subjects leave later syllabus content until the spring, so a student can sit a mock on material the course has not reached. A poor result there is information about the timetable rather than about ability. The useful part of a mock is the script, which shows where marks went, and that is worth considerably more than the grade on the front.

faqs.question: Which deadlines actually constrain a Diploma student in Al Karamah?
faqs.answer: The school's, almost always, because they are set weeks ahead of the board's to leave time for authenticity checks and marking. The board sets an upload or submission date; the school sets an earlier internal one. Missing the school's date rarely means a component goes unsubmitted, but it usually means the feedback round is lost, so the work reaches the board on time and unimproved. Ask your child's coordinator for the department's internal dates in writing at the start of the year.

faqs.question: When is the cheapest month to arrange support in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: The autumn, by a wide margin, because specialist capacity exists across almost every subject and a family has genuine choice of tutor and hour. From January, as mock results land across the emirate, demand rises sharply, and by February and March every cohort wants the same weeks. Autumn support can also still change content and, for an IGCSE student in Year 10, still influence the tier entry. Later support works inside whatever has already been decided.

faqs.question: Can a resit in November fix a disappointing June result?
faqs.answer: It depends on what the grade is needed for, which makes it a calendar calculation rather than an academic one. UAE candidates sit Cambridge and Edexcel in November, and the result arrives in the following January: November 2025 Edexcel results reached students on 22 January 2026. A sixth-form place starting in September cannot wait for that; a university application the following year can. Decide against the actual deadline before committing, and confirm entry dates through the school's examinations officer.

faqs.question: Is there a spring sitting in the UAE we could use instead?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge offers its February and March series to India only, so UAE candidates sit June and November. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. A number of tutoring pages written for UAE parents state otherwise, and that is the kind of error a family acts on by planning an entry around a date that does not exist for them. Always confirm against the live official timetable on the board's own website.

faqs.question: How should a block be arranged so that Ramadan does not wreck it?
faqs.answer: Decide before the month starts rather than during it. The two workable options are moving the slot into the post-Iftar window, which many Al Karamah families find better than a normal-term evening because the school day is short and the homework load lighter, or pausing for the month and resuming afterwards with the skipped sessions counted out of the block. What does not work is keeping the original hour and hoping, which produces missed sessions and then an unnecessary conversation about commitment.

faqs.question: Why count sessions rather than weeks for a tutoring block?
faqs.answer: Because the UAE year removes teaching time from every twelve-week plan. Ramadan changes the usable hour, Eid removes days, the winter break removes weeks, and during the series itself new content is pointless. A block billed across twelve calendar weeks that delivers eight teaching sessions is a quiet and common disappointment. Agreeing the session count and the skipped weeks in advance means the review at session eight compares the same quantity of teaching on both sides.

faqs.question: Our DP1 child has no exams this year. Can support wait until DP2?
faqs.answer: It can, and that is usually the expensive choice. DP1 carries no external examination, which makes it feel unpressured, while 20 to 30 per cent of each subject grade sits in internal assessment largely produced in DP1 or early DP2. The Exploration, the Scientific Investigation and the Extended Essay all have school deadlines that cluster in the first half of DP2. Booking the internal assessment block in the autumn of DP1 is the single decision that prevents the DP2 pile-up.

faqs.question: How do we build a revision timetable that actually survives?
faqs.answer: Allocate hours by the marked script rather than evenly across nine subjects, because equal slots burn time on comfortable revision. Build on three realistic evenings and a weekend morning rather than five free evenings, counting mandatory Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies homework in the load. Treat Thursday evening as lost. Then count the usable weeks between now and the papers using your school's published term dates, and plan on that number rather than on a generic twelve.

faqs.question: What is the Cambridge timetable zone issue we keep hearing about?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and the timetable differs between them. Cambridge's own guidance states it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong version. Your school manages this. If you are building a revision schedule from a timetable you downloaded yourself, confirm the zone with the examinations officer first. Five minutes against an irreversible risk.

faqs.question: Can one household run an IGCSE Year 11 and a DP1 plan at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, with two separate matches and a stagger. The subjects, boards and levels differ, so a single tutor covering both means one child gets the weaker match. What can be shared is the structure: the same written note after each session, the same error-log discipline and the same review at session eight for both. Stagger the slots by an hour rather than running two video lessons simultaneously in different rooms, which produces better work from both children.

faqs.question: Does the time of day matter more during the revision term?
faqs.answer: Considerably more, because every spare hour now has a purpose and a missed session cannot be made up. Families whose children travel out to Khalifa City or the mainland corridor almost always end up on a weekend morning once revision starts, which is also the slot that survives mock season. For island schools the best weekday window tends to be seven to half past eight, after a break and a meal, rather than immediately after the bell.

faqs.question: What evidence should we expect at the end of an eight-session block?
faqs.answer: Two marked scripts, a written list of causes from the first and a comparison against the second, and an error log showing which mistakes were addressed. From that the decision is straightforward: continue, change focus, change tutor, or finish. If nothing has moved, either the plan targeted the wrong gap or the match is wrong, and both are our problem to fix. An impression offered instead of a script is not evidence, whatever confidence it is delivered with.

intro.heading: The school run decides whether tutoring works
paragraphs: A tutoring plan in Al Khalidiyah fails for logistical reasons far more often than academic ones. The tutor knows the syllabus, the student needs the help, and by week five the session has moved twice, been cancelled once, and now sits at an hour when nobody in the house is capable of algebra. The reason is almost always that the slot was chosen to suit an adult's diary rather than the shape of a child's day.

That shape is specific in this district. Al Khalidiyah sits in the dense western-central band of Abu Dhabi island, within minutes of several long-established schools and within a bridge crossing of several newer ones. A child at a school in Al Bateen or Al Mushrif is home quickly. A child travelling to Saadiyat Island, Al Reem Island or the Khalifa City corridor is not, and the school bus adds its own time at both ends because it collects a route rather than a passenger. Two families on the same street can therefore have completely different workable session windows.

Then the day fills further. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside the licensed international curriculum, so the timetable carries more subjects than the examination entry list suggests, and homework follows. Add a sport, a music lesson or a Quran class and the genuinely free evening hours reduce to one or two. A tutoring plan that does not account for this is competing with homework rather than supporting it. Parents frequently discover this only after a month, when the session has quietly become the thing that gets dropped whenever the week is full, and the pattern then reads as a lack of commitment rather than a scheduling error made at the start.

This is the strongest practical argument for online delivery, and it has nothing to do with technology. A video session at a fixed hour does not depend on anyone crossing the island in late-afternoon traffic, so it does not move when Corniche Road is slow or when a tutor's earlier visit overran. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. Every UAE session runs one-to-one over live video with a shared screen.

The rest of this page is the scheduling and calendar information an Al Khalidiyah family actually needs: when the day realistically ends depending on where the school is, which schools this district feeds and which boards they run, how to run an IGCSE Year 11 and a DP1 sibling in the same household, the UAE academic year and the weeks that quietly disappear from it, both boards' examination calendars read backwards, and the honest test of whether a tutor is the right answer at all.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE, Years 10 and 11
programmes.description: Graded 9 to 1, with Core and Extended tiers in many subjects, and typically six to ten subjects taken. programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Tiered Foundation and Higher in mathematics and the sciences, graded 9 to 1, with some subjects available in a modular structure. Mathematics A, code 4MA1, runs two papers of two hours weighted equally, which is a different revision shape from Cambridge's 35 and 65 per cent split.
programmes.countryNote: Edexcel International GCSE series run in May/June and November. The tail between sitting and results is long: June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service, scored out of 45. Every subject carries an internally assessed component worth between 20 and 30 per cent, which means a significant share of the result is settled before any paper is sat.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi IB schools sit the May session, with November as the alternative route. We do not publish IB examination or results dates, because ibo.org blocks automated checking and an unverified date a family plans around is worse than none. Confirm with your school's IB coordinator.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four assessment criteria per subject, each out of eight, with command terms that reward explanation over recall. The Personal Project in Year 10 or 11 is the first substantial independent piece. Some island schools run MYP where others run IGCSE, so siblings at different schools may sit entirely different systems.
programmes.countryNote: Al Khalidiyah families comparing schools often find one running MYP to Year 11 and another running IGCSE. Neither is better in the abstract; they produce different preparation for the Diploma, and the MYP extended mathematics strand in particular feeds Analysis and Approaches.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-k.subjectsIntro: A household running two boards needs tutoring described by board and level rather than by subject name alone. The IB Diploma subjects below are the ones most requested from Abu Dhabi island, with the IGCSE grid following.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: SL sits Papers 1 and 2 at 40 per cent each with the Exploration at 20; HL adds Paper 3 and shifts the split to 30, 30, 20 and 20. Paper 1 is non-calculator, which exposes algebraic weakness immediately. Method marks are awarded separately from answers throughout.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Calculator-active, built on statistics, probability, modelling and, at Higher Level, matrices and graph theory. The interpretation demand is higher than students expect: a correct value earns little without a sentence saying what it means in the given context.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Paper 1 multiple choice, Paper 2 structured response, and the Scientific Investigation at 20 per cent. Energetics sign conventions, equilibrium reasoning and organic mechanism arrows are the recurring losses, with uncertainty treatment in practical work close behind.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Derivation-heavy, with graph gradients read for physical quantities. Students who can state a formula often cannot name the assumption that makes it valid, which is where explanation marks go. Circular motion and capacitance at Higher Level are predictable trouble spots.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Large content volume concealing a single skill: applying a named process to an unfamiliar context under command-term discipline. Genetics, plant transport and statistical treatment in the Scientific Investigation account for most of the difference between bands.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three Internal Assessment commentaries of 800 words each on recent news articles, plus papers that reward a fully labelled diagram and a developed evaluation. Unlabelled axes and conclusions that restate the analysis are the two commonest avoidable losses.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis in Paper 1, comparative essay in Paper 2, an internally assessed Individual Oral, and at Higher Level an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words. Paper 1 marks are lost to summary where analysis of effect was required.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: The TOK essay runs to 1,600 words on a prescribed title, with an exhibition of three objects and commentaries totalling up to 950 words. The Extended Essay is 4,000 words marked out of 34, with Critical Thinking alone worth 12. Both contribute to the three bonus points.

igcseSubjects.description: 0580 Extended is Paper 2 at 35 per cent and Paper 4 at 65; 4MA1 Higher is two equally weighted two-hour papers. Premature rounding, histograms with unequal class widths and bearings not stated to three figures are the reliable losses.

igcseSubjects.description: Electricity and waves dominate the lost marks, usually through confusion between series and parallel reasoning. The alternative-to-practical paper rewards knowing how apparatus is arranged, which theory notes alone cannot supply.

sections.heading: Where does the Al Khalidiyah day actually end?
paragraphs: The honest answer depends on the school, and the spread is wider than parents of children at the same school realise. A child at a campus in Al Bateen or Al Mushrif can be home within fifteen or twenty minutes of the final bell. A child bussed to Khalifa City or Mussafah may not walk through the door until well after four, because a bus runs a route rather than a journey and collects half a neighbourhood on the way. Between those two cases sits a full hour of difference, and it changes which session hours are real.

After arrival there is a gap that families routinely forget to count. A teenager who gets home at four needs food, a change of clothes and a genuine pause before anything useful happens. Starting a tutoring session at half past four produces a student who is physically present and cognitively still on the bus. The scripts from those sessions are visibly worse than the same student's work at seven, which is why the later slot usually wins even though the earlier one feels more disciplined.

Then the week has its own rhythm. Thursday evening in the UAE carries a weekend feeling and is the worst weekday slot in most households. Sunday evening, at the start of the working week, is often the best, because homework volume has not yet accumulated. Mid-week evenings after a sports fixture or a music lesson are unreliable regardless of intention. A plan that acknowledges this holds; one that treats all five evenings as equivalent does not.

sections.heading: Which schools this neighbourhood feeds, and which boards they run
paragraphs: Al Khalidiyah is not a single-school catchment. Families on the same street send children to campuses on the island, across a bridge and out on the mainland, and those campuses run different curricula. One household can therefore be managing a Cambridge IGCSE Year 11, an IB Middle Years Programme Year 9 and a Diploma Programme DP1 simultaneously, which is three different assessment systems with three different deadline calendars.

That matters for tutoring in a very practical way. A tutor who prepares Cambridge 0580 is not automatically the right person for IB Analysis and Approaches, and neither is automatically right for an MYP Year 9 student being marked against four criteria out of eight. Asking a single tutor to cover all three means two of your children get the weaker match. Separate matches, coordinated scheduling, is the arrangement that actually works.

It also matters for expectations. An IGCSE year ends in a defined series of papers; a Diploma year is a two-year structure with internal assessment deadlines spread through it; an MYP year is continuous criterion-referenced assessment with no external examination. Parents who apply one mental model to all three become frustrated, usually with the child who happens to be in the system they understand least.

Private schools in the emirate are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which publishes its own inspection outcomes. That is the only common scale on which two schools in different curricula can be compared, and it is named by almost none of the competing tutoring pages for Abu Dhabi. Treat a rating as background about a school rather than information about a particular class in a particular year.

sections.heading: Running an IGCSE Year 11 and a DP1 in the same household
paragraphs: This is a common Al Khalidiyah situation and it is harder than two separate plans, because the two systems peak at different moments and compete for the same evenings. The Year 11 student has a single examination series looming, with revision pressure concentrating in the months before it. The DP1 student has no external examination that year at all, which makes their work feel less urgent and means it is quietly neglected until the internal assessment deadlines in DP2 arrive all at once.

The sequencing answer is to treat the Year 11 series as the fixed point and build the DP1 plan around it, with one caveat. The DP1 year contains the Mathematical Exploration or its equivalent in other subjects, and that component carries twenty per cent of a grade. Starting it late because a sibling's examinations dominated the household is the single most expensive consequence of poor coordination, and it is entirely avoidable by booking the Exploration block in the autumn.

Practically, two children need two slots and should not share one. Shared sessions sound economical and deliver two half-lessons, because the content, board and level differ. What can genuinely be shared is the structure: the same written note after each session, the same error-log discipline, the same eight-week review point for both. That makes the household manageable without pretending the academic work is interchangeable.

The other thing worth coordinating is the quiet hour. In an apartment, two simultaneous video sessions in different rooms is workable with headphones and not ideal. Staggering them by an hour usually produces better work from both children and less friction in between, which is a scheduling observation rather than an academic one and matters more than it should.

sections.heading: The UAE academic year and the weeks that quietly disappear
paragraphs: A tutoring plan is usually costed in weeks and delivered in fewer. The UAE academic year contains several predictable interruptions, and a family that plans around them keeps the rhythm, while one that does not loses a month and concludes that tutoring does not work for them.

Ramadan is the largest. School days shorten, the working rhythm shifts, and evening energy moves to the hours after Iftar. A fixed six o'clock session that worked in January becomes the worst hour available. For many Al Khalidiyah families the post-Iftar window is genuinely better than anything in a normal term, because the house is awake, the school day was short and the homework backlog is lighter. For others the right answer is to pause and resume afterwards. Both work as decisions; neither works as a drift.

The other gaps are more ordinary and equally disruptive. Eid breaks, the long winter holiday, National Day weekends, half-terms and school-specific closures. Then there is examination season itself, when a student should be sitting papers rather than taking lessons, and when a sensible plan reduces rather than intensifies. A tutoring block billed across twelve weeks that actually contains eight teaching weeks is the commonest quiet disappointment in this market.

The fix is to count the teaching weeks at the start, agree in advance which ones will be skipped, and set the review point by session number rather than by calendar date. Eight sessions is eight sessions, whether they take ten weeks or fourteen. Measuring by sessions rather than by months also makes the eight-week review honest, because both sides are comparing the same quantity of teaching.

sections.heading: Both boards' examination calendars, counted backwards
paragraphs: Nobody in the researched competitor set publishes an examination calendar at all. The word November returned zero hits across every fetchable page, which for a market where candidates sit a November series is a remarkable omission. Reading the calendar backwards is more useful than reading it forwards, because it shows which weeks are genuinely decisive and which are not.

For Cambridge, UAE candidates sit the June and November series. The February and March series is offered to India only, and several pages aimed at UAE parents get this wrong, which matters because an entry deadline is something a family acts on. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Your school's examinations officer holds the right version.

For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, series run in May/June and November, with provisional timetables published ahead of each. The results tail is long and worth planning around: June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those are backward-looking citations, included because they make the pattern checkable rather than because they predict a future date.

For the IB Diploma, Abu Dhabi schools sit the May session with November as the alternative. We publish no IB dates on this page: ibo.org blocks automated checking, and an unverified session or results date that a family plans around is worse than no date. Confirm with your school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org directly. What can be said without a date is the shape: internal assessment deadlines, the Extended Essay submission and mock examinations all land in the months before the papers, and they compete with each other.

sections.heading: Homework, school support, and when a tutor is genuinely the answer
paragraphs: Not every struggling student needs a tutor, and a page that pretended otherwise would be selling rather than advising. There are three cheaper things to try first, and in Al Khalidiyah households they are frequently skipped because they require a conversation with the school rather than a payment.

The first is the school's own support. Most schools in the emirate run some form of after-school clinic, departmental help or targeted intervention, and it is free. A parent who asks the head of department directly, naming the specific topic rather than the general worry, often gets a useful answer and sometimes gets the problem solved. The second is the homework environment: a student working on a sofa with a phone nearby is not working, and fixing that changes more than an hour a week of tutoring will.

The third is diagnosis without purchase. Ask the school what the last assessment was marked against and which specific marks were lost. If the answer is detailed, you may not need anybody. If the answer is a grade and a general comment, you have learned something about why your child cannot explain the problem either.

A tutor becomes the right answer in three situations. When the gap is specific and the school cannot give it individual time, which is most of them. When the problem is examination technique rather than content, because that requires marked scripts and one-to-one discussion that a class of twenty-five cannot provide. And when the student has lost confidence to the point where they will not ask questions in class, which is a genuine and common reason, and one that a patient hour a week with the same adult addresses better than anything else available.

sections.heading: Buses, transport and the hour a teenager can actually think in
paragraphs: School transport is the hidden variable in every Al Khalidiyah tutoring plan. A bus is scheduled around a route, not around your child, which means the journey home is routinely longer than the journey in and considerably longer than a parent's own drive would be. Forty-five minutes on a bus after a full school day is not neutral time; it is additional fatigue, and the session booked immediately afterwards pays for it.

Families who switch from the earliest possible slot to one an hour later are frequently surprised by the difference in output. The same student, the same tutor, the same material, and visibly better scripts. There is nothing mysterious about it: a tired teenager processes slowly and makes the kind of careless errors that then get mistaken for a content gap. Several of the diagnostic sessions we see described as revealing weak algebra are in fact revealing a student who started at half past four.

The second transport consideration is the end of the session rather than the start. An in-home arrangement requires a tutor to arrive and leave, which in practice means the session's edges are soft: a late start because of traffic, an early finish because of the next visit. An online slot has hard edges. That reliability is worth more over a term than any single lesson's quality, because consistency is the mechanism by which tutoring works at all.

For families whose children travel furthest, the honest recommendation is often a weekend morning plus one short weekday session, rather than two weekday evenings that will both be fought for. It is less tidy and it holds up through mock season, which is the only test that matters.

sections.heading: What starting looks like, and what we agree before any money moves
paragraphs: The first conversation should be short and should produce three facts: the board and level for each child, the hours that are genuinely free once the school run and activities are counted, and the specific thing that prompted the call. The third is the one families under-describe. "Struggling with maths" is a feeling; "lost half the marks on the statistics section of the mock" is a brief.

Then a free trial lesson, with no card required and no commitment attached, built around a past-paper diagnostic rather than an introductory chat. The purpose is twofold: the student judges whether the tutor's explanation lands, and the tutor produces evidence of where the marks are going. You should finish the trial with a short written read that separates genuine content gaps from process losses like rounding, misread command words and timing.

Next, the slot and the measure. A standing weekly hour in Gulf Standard Time, agreed as movable in advance because the year is not uniform, plus one thing we will both examine after eight sessions, usually a timed paper marked against the published scheme. Counting in sessions rather than weeks matters in the UAE calendar, where Ramadan, Eid and school closures remove teaching weeks from any twelve-week block.

Finally, the end. At the eight-session review the options are to continue, change focus, change tutor, or finish, and finishing is a real option we will name when the work is done. If the second script has not moved, either the plan targeted the wrong gap or the match is wrong, and both are ours to fix. What we will not do is promise a grade, publish an invented price list, or claim an accreditation. IB Gram holds no approval, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson.

faqs.question: What time can we realistically start a session if the school bus gets in at four?
faqs.answer: Allow an hour. A teenager off a forty-five minute bus run needs food, a change and a genuine pause before anything useful happens, so a half past four start produces a student who is present and still mentally on the bus. Half past five is the earliest that tends to work, and six to seven thirty produces noticeably better scripts. Families who move the slot an hour later are frequently surprised, because the errors that disappear were fatigue rather than a content gap.

faqs.question: Which evening of the week is the worst for a tutoring session in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Thursday, by a clear margin. The weekend feeling arrives early in the UAE week and a Thursday evening session is attended rather than used. Friday is generally reserved by agreement. The strongest weekday slots are Sunday and Monday, when the week has started but homework has not yet accumulated. Saturday morning is the single most reliable slot in the whole week, and it is the one that survives mock season when every weekday evening collapses.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both our Year 11 and our DP1 child?
faqs.answer: Only if the subject, board and level genuinely line up, which is rare. A Cambridge 0580 Extended candidate and an Analysis and Approaches SL student are sitting different examinations with different mark schemes, and a tutor strong in one is not automatically strong in the other. Asking for one person usually means one child gets the weaker match. What can be shared is the structure: the same written notes, the same error-log discipline and the same review point for both children.

faqs.question: Does anybody actually travel to Al Khalidiyah for lessons?
faqs.answer: Not through us. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. Every session runs one-to-one online over live video with a shared screen. Beyond cost, the practical gain is reliability: an online slot has hard edges, while a visit has soft ones, arriving late because of traffic and finishing early because of the next appointment. Over a term, consistency moves more marks than any single excellent lesson.

faqs.question: How many teaching weeks does a twelve-week plan actually contain in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Often eight or nine. Ramadan changes the usable hour, Eid removes days, the winter break removes weeks, and examination season removes the point of new content. A block billed across twelve calendar weeks that delivers eight teaching sessions is the quietest disappointment in this market. The fix is to count sessions rather than weeks, agree at the start which weeks will be skipped, and set the review point at a session number so both sides compare the same amount of teaching.

faqs.question: Our son's school has an after-school maths clinic. Do we still need a tutor?
faqs.answer: Possibly not, and it is worth exhausting first because it is free. Ask the head of department about the specific topic rather than the general worry, and ask what the last assessment was marked against and which marks were lost. If you get a detailed answer, the school may solve it. A tutor earns its place when the gap needs individual time the class cannot give, when the problem is examination technique rather than content, or when a student has stopped asking questions in class.

faqs.question: Which schools do Al Khalidiyah families actually use?
faqs.answer: A wide spread rather than one catchment. Children from the same street attend campuses in Al Bateen and Al Mushrif on the island, across the bridge on Saadiyat and Al Reem, and out on the mainland in Khalifa City and Mussafah. Those schools run British, American, IB and Indian curricula, which is why one household can be managing a Cambridge IGCSE, an MYP year and a Diploma year at once. All private schools in the emirate are licensed and inspected by ADEK.

faqs.question: Is there a February sitting we could use if the summer series goes wrong?
faqs.answer: Not for UAE candidates. Cambridge offers its February and March series to India only, so UAE students sit June and November. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. A resit after a summer sitting therefore points at November rather than the following spring, and the entry deadline sits months before the paper. Several tutoring pages written for UAE parents state this wrongly, which matters because it is a date a family plans around.

faqs.question: Why will you not print the IB exam dates on this page?
faqs.answer: Because we could not verify them. The IB's own site returns an error to automated checking, which means any IB session or results date we published would be taken from a secondary source and presented as fact. A wrong date that a family plans a revision schedule around is worse than no date at all, especially inside an answer a voice assistant might read back. Abu Dhabi schools sit the May session; confirm the window and results day with your school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org.

faqs.question: What happens to our slot during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: It moves, and we agree that before the term starts rather than during it. School days shorten, the rhythm shifts, and the evening energy sits after Iftar, so a six o'clock session becomes the worst hour of the day. Many island families find the post-Iftar window better than anything in a normal term, because the house is awake and the homework load is lighter. Others pause for the month and resume. Both work as decisions; neither works as a drift.

faqs.question: Are two short sessions better than one long one for a Year 10 student?
faqs.answer: Frequently, yes. Two forty-five minute sessions on different evenings suit a younger student or anyone whose concentration falls away after half an hour, and they cost the same as one longer session. The second advantage is contact frequency: a misunderstanding gets caught within days rather than within a week. For a DP2 student working through full timed papers the opposite is true, because a paper needs a single uninterrupted block plus marking time.

faqs.question: Does it matter that mandatory Arabic and Islamic lessons fill the timetable?
faqs.answer: It matters to your scheduling rather than to the tutoring itself. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside the licensed international curriculum, so the week carries more subjects than the examination entry list suggests and the homework follows. In practice that pushes the workable session later into the evening, which is usually where better scripts come from anyway, so the constraint is less damaging than it first appears.

faqs.question: How do we judge whether the arrangement is working, with two children on different plans?
faqs.answer: Use the same mechanism for both and compare each child against themselves. A timed paper for each at the start, marked against the published scheme rather than impressionistically, repeated after eight sessions. Between them, a short written note after every session and an error log so no mistake is taught twice. Comparing the two children against each other tells you nothing useful, because they are sitting different examinations with different mark schemes and different timescales.

faqs.question: What will you not do, even if we ask?
faqs.answer: We will not promise a grade, because nobody can. We will not draft an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or TOK essay; a tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on work the student wrote, and anything further is academic malpractice that falls on the student. We will not claim approval, accreditation or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, because IB Gram holds none. And we will not publish a figure we cannot source.

intro.heading: Start with the monthly number, not the hourly one
paragraphs: Almost every tutoring conversation in Abu Dhabi begins with an hourly rate, and almost every budgeting mistake follows from it. An hourly figure tells you very little on its own. What a family in Al Manaseer actually commits to is a monthly amount, repeated for eight or nine months, sometimes twice over because there are two children in two curricula. That is the number worth establishing first, and it is the number nobody publishes.

So here are the published monthly figures from this market. Around AED 799 a month buys eight online sessions. In-home packages built from four two-hour visits are advertised at AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for a single weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle band, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. A Year 13 Higher Level subject sits in that top band, and a household supporting one Diploma child and one IGCSE child can reach AED 2,500 a month without anyone having made an extravagant decision.

Those are market figures published by providers, not an IB Gram price list. They are useful because they let you sanity-check a quote. If a provider will not give you a monthly number for a defined plan, you are not comparing like with like, and three of the six competitor pages researched for this project publish no price at all while two quote in US dollars, a currency no UAE family transacts in. Insisting on a monthly figure is the one move that makes three quotes comparable.

The next thing to understand is where the money goes rather than how much of it there is. In-home one-to-one visits in the UAE are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, against AED 150 to 300 for comparable teaching delivered online. The difference is not a quality premium. It is petrol, parking and a tutor's evening spent crossing Abu Dhabi island twice. Al Manaseer sits between Al Khalidiyah and Al Bateen, which is a convenient address and still a thirty-minute round trip from most places a specialist might live.

IB Gram does not sell in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; visits to a family's address are a service we run only in India. Al Manaseer lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. What that removes from the invoice is the journey, and what it adds is a tutor chosen for the subject rather than the postcode. The rest of this page is about the four places a two-curriculum household loses money, what to send when you ask three providers for a quote, and the two money questions nobody in this market answers straight.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-m.programmesIntro: Cost behaves differently in each programme stage, and an Al Manaseer household often has children in two of them at once. Knowing which stage is expensive and which is cheap changes where the money should go.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The cheapest stage to intervene in and the one most often skipped. Criterion-based reports rarely look alarming, so a gap that would cost a few hundred dirhams to close in Year 9 goes untouched and reappears as a specialist-rate problem in Year 12. Sessions here sit in the lower market bands because the teaching required is less specialised.
programmes.countryNote: Al Manaseer families with a child in MYP usually have them at a campus on Al Reem Island, Saadiyat Island or along Al Raha, and the Personal Project in the final MYP year is the point at which families first discover what an internally assessed task does to a household timetable.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: The middle band in cost terms, with eight or nine subjects competing for the same budget. The decisive spend is early: a Year 10 tier block at AED 150 to 300 an hour prevents a Year 11 recovery programme at the same rate for three times as many hours. Spending concentrated in April of Year 11 is the most expensive pattern available.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi candidates sit the Cambridge June and November series, with the February and March series offered to India only. Entry is submitted by the school months ahead, so a tier the family wanted to change has usually stopped being changeable by the time the budget conversation happens.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The expensive stage. Six subjects, an Internal Assessment in each, plus the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge, and Higher Level specialists sit at the top of the published bands at AED 200 to 450 and above. Bestimate's exam-year monthly estimate of AED 1,000 to 2,000 plus is describing exactly this student.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students from Al Manaseer travel to IB campuses across Abu Dhabi, where Higher Level cohorts are small. Scarcity at the top of the market is real, which is why booking a specialist in September costs less than finding one in March, when the people with capacity are those nobody else wanted.

abu-dhabi/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-m.subjectsIntro: Cost per useful hour varies sharply by subject and component. These are the ones Al Manaseer households most often buy, with a note on where the money works hardest.

subjects.name: IB Mathematics AA and AI
subjects.description: Higher Level sits at the top of the published rate bands because the teaching pool is small. The best value inside the subject is non-calculator technique and early exploration work, both cheap in hours and heavily weighted in marks.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.description: Mid-band rates and the clearest early-spending case in the whole set. A Year 10 block aimed at the tier decision costs a fraction of a Year 11 recovery programme and has a larger effect on the final grade.

subjects.name: IB Chemistry and Physics
subjects.description: Among the most expensive Diploma subjects to staff well at Higher Level, and the ones where a generalist is exposed fastest. The Internal Assessment is where the money works hardest, if it is spent in the autumn rather than the week before submission.

subjects.name: IGCSE Sciences
subjects.description: Good value because the mark loss is concentrated in recall precision, units, significant figures and experimental description, all of which respond to a handful of targeted sessions rather than a term of general revision.

subjects.name: IB English A and English B
subjects.description: Two different courses with different assessments including the Individual Oral. The expensive mistake here is structural: a student in the wrong course needs support for two years, which dwarfs any hourly rate difference between providers.

subjects.name: IGCSE English Language and Literature
subjects.description: Essay structure under timing is the limiting factor, which makes a longer weekend session once a fortnight better value than a short weeknight hour. Vocabulary work is the least cost-effective thing to buy in this subject.

subjects.name: IB Economics and Business Management
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and evaluation command terms carry the marks. Internal Assessment commentaries have strict word limits, and exceeding them is an avoidable loss that costs nothing to prevent and cannot be repaired afterwards.

subjects.name: Internal Assessment and Extended Essay coaching
subjects.description: The highest-leverage hours in the Diploma when bought early, and close to worthless when bought late. Criteria taught with their mark allocations, topics interrogated for depth, feedback on the student's own drafts, and nothing written for them.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A small field of specialists, so availability rather than price is the constraint. Households that need it should ask early in Year 12 rather than in the term the essay is due, when the few people who teach it are already committed.

subjects.name: Diagnostic sessions across subjects
subjects.description: One hour per candidate subject, each ending in a written gap list. For a household choosing between three subjects to fund, this is dramatically cheaper than buying packages in all three and learning the answer in March.

sections.heading: What a month of tutoring costs in central Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: A month of one weekly hour of qualified online tuition in this market costs between roughly AED 600 and AED 1,200 according to Bestimate's 2026 estimates, rising to AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. At the budget end, where university-student and generalist online tutors sit, the same weekly hour is estimated at AED 240 to AED 600. Published package prices put eight online sessions at around AED 799 a month, and four in-home two-hour visits at AED 1,599 to AED 1,799.

Those are the numbers an Al Manaseer household should budget against, and the table sets them out so a quote can be checked against them. Two things are worth noticing. The in-home monthly package costs roughly double the online one for the same number of contact hours, and the specialist exam-year band costs roughly triple the budget band. Neither gap is about teaching quality in a simple way: the first is travel, and the second is scarcity at the top of a small market.

The second thing is that a household with two children in two curricula is looking at two of these lines, not one. That is where a reasonable set of individual decisions becomes an unreasonable total. The practical response is not to buy cheaper hours but to buy fewer, better-aimed ones, which is what the rest of this page is about. A single diagnostic hour that redirects a year's spending is the best-value purchase in the entire table.

sections.heading: What the in-home premium actually buys
paragraphs: The gap between AED 150 to 300 an hour online and AED 180 to 500 in-home is real money, and it deserves an honest accounting rather than a sales line. In-home tutoring is a genuine service with genuine advantages: a younger child stays in a familiar room, a parent overhears the teaching, and nothing depends on a connection. For some families that is worth the premium and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

What the premium buys, though, is mostly transport. A tutor crossing Abu Dhabi island to reach a block in Al Manaseer at seven in the evening spends perhaps an hour travelling for one hour taught, and that hour has to be paid for by somebody. It usually arrives as a higher hourly rate, a two-hour minimum booking nobody needs, or both. The two-hour minimum is the costlier of the two, because concentration on technical material degrades after about seventy-five minutes and the second hour of a weeknight double is frequently the least productive time a household pays for all year.

There is a second, quieter cost: the shortlist. A tutor who must physically reach Al Manaseer can serve a radius of a few kilometres, and for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level or Diploma chemistry that radius often contains one or two people. If neither is a specialist, the family pays the premium and receives a generalist. The table compares the formats on the terms that matter to a budget rather than to a brochure.

sections.heading: The four places a two-curriculum household overspends
paragraphs: Overspending on tutoring in Al Manaseer is rarely about the hourly rate. It is about buying hours in the wrong order, in the wrong subject, or twice over. Four patterns recur in households running an IGCSE child and a Diploma child at once, and each has a price attached.

The first is running three or four subjects concurrently. A household worried about maths, chemistry and English buys all three, and each receives a third of an already short week. Sequencing them, one per term, costs a third as much and works better because the student has capacity to absorb one intervention at a time. The second is duplicating support: an older sibling's tutor retained out of loyalty for a younger child on a different specification, which is a specification mismatch nobody notices until a mock paper.

The third is buying packages before any diagnosis. A ten-hour block looks like a discount, but if six hours go on topics the student already holds, the effective rate on the useful four is more than double the sticker price. One diagnostic hour per candidate subject, each ending in a written gap list, is the cheapest way to redirect a year's budget. The fourth is late Internal Assessment support in the Diploma. The mark ceiling is set by the topic and the depth of mathematics or science available in it, both decided in the first fortnight. A tutor engaged in the final week is reading a finished piece at the same hourly rate for a fraction of the effect.

sections.heading: Tutoring in the context of the whole education bill
paragraphs: A tutoring budget looks very different beside a school fee than it does on its own, and the context is worth establishing once rather than argued about every term. Dubai's private school sector, the best documented in the country, served 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen different curricula, with the UK curriculum taking the largest share of enrolment, followed by Indian, then US, then International Baccalaureate.

On fees, KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for private schools in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6%. Abu Dhabi's fee regime is set separately under ADEK, so these Dubai figures are context rather than a direct read-across.

Set a tutoring plan against that. One weekly mid-band hour at AED 600 to 1,200 a month across nine months is a meaningful sum, and it is usually a small fraction of an international school fee for the same year. That is not an argument for spending freely; it is an argument for spending deliberately, because the marginal return on one well-aimed tutoring hour is frequently higher than the marginal return on anything else in the education budget. sections.heading: Cheap help that works, and expensive help that does not
paragraphs: Not every low rate is false economy and not every high rate buys something. The useful distinction is between work that needs a specialist and work that does not, and a household that gets this right spends less and achieves more than one that simply pays up everywhere.

Work that a budget-band tutor handles perfectly well: supervised practice in a subject the student basically understands, Key Stage 3 and Middle Years consolidation, times tables and arithmetic fluency, reading through worked solutions, and keeping a student moving through routine syllabus coverage in a Standard Level subject sitting comfortably at a 5. Paying AED 350 an hour for any of that is paying for a qualification the task does not require.

Work that needs the specialist band: Higher Level Diploma teaching, Internal Assessment and Extended Essay coaching, the extended-response Paper 3, IGCSE tier diagnosis where the entry decision is live, and mock-script dissection where the value depends entirely on the reader knowing the mark scheme. Expensive help that reliably does not work, meanwhile, has a short list of its own: two-hour weeknight blocks, general revision bought in the final fortnight, homework supervision at specialist rates, and any package purchased before anybody looked at a marked script. The rule of thumb is simple enough to apply at a kitchen table. If the task needs somebody to know the mark scheme, buy the specialist. If it needs somebody to sit beside a student and keep them working, do not.

sections.heading: What to send when you ask three providers for a quote
paragraphs: Comparing tutoring quotes in Abu Dhabi is unusually difficult because providers answer different questions. One quotes per hour, another per session of unstated length, a third per month with the number of sessions buried, and a fourth declines to quote at all until a call has been booked. The fix is to send all three the same brief, so the replies are comparable.

A good brief is six lines. The curriculum and level, named precisely: IB Diploma Analysis and Approaches Higher Level, or Cambridge IGCSE 0580 Extended, not maths. The year group and the school. Which specific thing you want help with, if you know. The two evening windows that genuinely work from Al Manaseer. How many weeks you expect to run for. And a direct request: give me a monthly figure for a defined plan, with session length stated.

Then ask the same three closing questions of everybody. Does the quoted price include VAT, which is a question only the provider can answer for their own pricing and one worth asking in writing? What happens if we stop after one session? And who, by name, will teach my child, and which courses and levels have they actually taught? The table below is the checklist. Any provider who cannot answer all of it has told you something useful about what the arrangement will be like in February. Send all three briefs on the same day, too. Availability changes week to week in this market, and a reply received a fortnight after the others is answering a different question about capacity.

sections.heading: Free trials, and the conditions worth reading
paragraphs: Almost every provider in this market offers a free trial, and the word free does different work in different offers. Reading the condition before booking costs nothing and occasionally saves a month's fees, so it is worth doing once properly.

The questions are short. How long is the trial, and is it a full session or a shortened one? Is a card required to book it? Is it genuinely a teaching session, or a consultation with a coordinator who then introduces a tutor later? Is the tutor who teaches the trial the tutor who continues? And if the trial does not suit, is anything owed, and does anything auto-renew? An offer that cannot answer those in writing is not an offer you can compare.

For clarity about what happens here: the IB Gram trial is a free, full working session with the tutor who would continue, named before the lesson together with the courses and levels they have taught. The tutor teaches something, tests a hypothesis about where the gap sits, and writes down what they found, and you receive that written gap list afterwards. If the fit is wrong, the match changes and nothing is owed. Nothing renews automatically off the back of a trial, because a mismatch identified in week one costs one hour and a mismatch tolerated until half term costs a term. One more worth asking: whether the trial is recorded or whether notes from it are shared with you. A trial that produces nothing you can read afterwards leaves you with an impression rather than information, and an impression is exactly what the next quote will be judged on.

sections.heading: The permit and the VAT question, answered as far as they can be
paragraphs: Two money questions come up constantly in this market and are almost never answered straight, so here is as much as can honestly be said about each.

The permit first, because it is the one with a clear answer. An individual giving private lessons in the UAE needs a private tuition work permit from MoHRE, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and that fact matters commercially: any provider implying that a licence fee is built into their rate is describing something that does not exist. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule is published, any figure circulating online is unverified.

VAT is the question that cannot be answered responsibly on a page like this. The UAE VAT treatment of tuition fees depends on the provider's own status and registration, and stating a general rule without a Federal Tax Authority citation would be guessing at a family's expense. The only useful thing is a practical instruction: ask every provider, in writing, whether their quoted AED figure includes VAT, and ask for their tax registration number if they claim to charge it. A provider who answers both clearly is easy to compare and a provider who deflects is not.

process.title: Write down the monthly number you can sustain

process.title: Pick one subject per child and sequence the rest
process.description: Fund the widest gap now and defer the others deliberately to later terms. One live commitment per child is what keeps the monthly figure where you set it and keeps the student able to absorb the help.

process.title: Take the free trial before committing anything
